metadata.title: Someone open-sourced Stripe Billing (Mistral uses it)
metadata.author: Indie Hacker News
metadata.shortDescription:
👉 Daily indie hacker news + AI deep dives for builders → https://indiehacker.news/yt

Stripe Billing keeps 0.7% of every invoice you send. Lago, the open-source billing engine behind Mistral AI and PayPal's merchant billing, gives the whole engine away, but "free" comes with a catch.

Here's what it actually does, how it stacks up against Stripe Billing, Metronome and Chargebee, and who should be paying attention.

🔗 Repo: https://github.com/getlago/lago
🌐 Site: https://www.getlago.com

CHAPTERS
00:00 Stripe's 0.7% cut
00:34 The README
01:03 Lago vs Stripe Billing
01:55 What you get
02:46 Under the hood
03:17 Self-hosting
03:36 v1.57.0
04:04 The catch
04:40 Verdict

Get every story like this in your inbox. Free daily newsletter: https://indiehacker.news/yt

#Lago #StripeBilling #OpenSource #UsageBasedBilling #SaaS #IndieHacker

segments.text: Stripe billing takes 0.7% of every
invoice you send. Lago gives the whole
billing engine away.
If you charge per token or per API call,
billing turns into a second product and
Stripe takes a cut of it forever.
Mistral and PayPal already bill through
Lago instead, and you can host it
yourself. It was built by people who'd
lived through billing hell inside a
bank. But free here doesn't mean what
you think, and there's a catch. I'll
show you what it does, how it stacks up
against the paid options, and that
catch.
Here's the README. Right under the logo,
there's a number. $829 million in
invoices issued every month. Scroll down
and a demo price is three AI requests,
input tokens and output tokens for 2
cents. Then one line sums up the whole
job. Usage events go in, invoices and
payments come out. And the customer
table near the bottom raises the obvious
question.
What are all those teams not paying
Stripe?
So what's the actual bill? Stripe
billing is 0.7% of your billing volume,
and that's on top of the card fees. Last
December, Stripe also agreed to buy
Metronome, the metering company behind a
lot of AI billing for a reported billion
dollars. Chargebee and Orb sell the same
idea as a subscription. Lago's pitch is
different. Keep Stripe or Adyen for
moving the money and stop renting the
part that decides what to charge. So
what do you actually get for free?
Enjoying this so far? Subscribe to the
YouTube channel and grab the free daily
newsletter at indiehacker.news.
New deep dive every weekday.
The repo numbers are modest for software
that sits on top of real money. The
backing is Y Combinator plus around led
by First Mark, and the license is the
part to remember for later.
Quick backstory on that bank. The
founders were early at Konto in France,
and their post calling billing a
nightmare for engineers hit the top of
Hacker News.
Lago is their fix, and it starts with
metering. You send an event every time a
customer burns tokens or hits your API,
and Lago dedupes those events by
transaction ID. So if your app retries a
request, nobody gets built twice.
Pricing sits on top of that.
Graduated tiers and packages can live in
the same plan as minimum commitments or
plane seats. Prepaid credits come with
wallets and automatic top ups, which is
how most AI companies sell now. And the
newest piece is agent access. There's an
MCP server and a CLI, so your coding
agent can read your invoices and usage
directly,
which raises a fair question about
what's running underneath.
Underneath, it's a Rails app that pushes
almost everything into background jobs
on Sidekiq and Redis. Postgres holds the
data, and a React dashboard sits on top,
while invoice PDFs come out of their own
separate service. For really heavy event
traffic, there's an events processor
written in Go.
Getting all of that running on your own
box is shorter than you'd expect.
Want to be featured? Pitch your open
source repo at indiehacker.news/apply
and get in front of thousands of
builders.
You clone it and generate one key. Then
Docker Compose brings the whole stack up
in one go. If you just want to watch it
build something, there's an example
script that runs that same token pricing
from the README against a throwaway
organization, all locally.
The latest release, though, says a lot
about where Lago is heading.
Version 1.57 shipped on November 5th,
and it's small. The all-in-one image now
builds on hardened Wolfi base images.
The release before that moved the
dashboard container off root and onto
port 8080. So check your reverse proxy
before you upgrade. And here's the funny
part. Two of the merged pull requests
came from ClaudeBots, and one of them
rewrote the README to push Lago Cloud as
the default, which brings us to the
catch.
So here's the catch. The open source
edition is AGPL, and Lago's own pricing
page calls it a limited feature set.
Single sign-on and audit logs sit behind
a commercial deal, and so do custom
roles. If you'd rather not run it, Lago
Cloud charges 0.7% of processed billings
after your first $100,000.
That's exactly Stripe's rate, and you
still pay card fees on top to move the
money. Self-hosting dodges that cut, but
then you own the uptime of the system
that decides what every customer owes
you. So who's this actually for?
My verdict, for an AI product that
builds on metered usage, this is the
self-hosted billing setup to take
seriously right now, as long as you're
willing to keep it running in
production.
The builder I'd handed to this week is
watching their payment provider's cut
grow with each new customer. Run the
demo tonight, and within an hour, you'll
know whether it fits your pricing.

If you'd rather not run it, Lago Cloud charges 0.7% of processed billings after your first $100,000. That's exactly Stripe's rate, and you still pay card fees on top to move the money. Self-hosting dodges that cut, but then you own the uptime of the system that decides what every customer owes you. So who's this actually for? My verdict, for an AI product that builds on metered usage, this is the self-hosted billing setup to take seriously right now, as long as you're willing to keep it running in production. The builder I'd handed to this week is watching their payment provider's cut grow with each new customer. Run the demo tonight, and within an hour, you'll know whether it fits your pricing.

Stripe and Metronome just launched billing for LLM tokens in public preview, and Stripe engineering manager Kimberly Hou walks through exactly how it works.
If your AI app calls multiple models and their prices keep changing, this is how you stop worrying about margins.

In this video, Kimberly Hou explains why pricing AI usage is so hard when customer usage varies and model prices change, then demos the full flow in a Metronome sandbox. She builds a rate card with her chosen models, sets a markup, and uses custom pricing units to bill customers in credits. metadata.title: Make Your AI Chatbot Pay For Itself — Stripe Usage Metering, Paywalls & Caps (Chat Data)
metadata.author: Medical Chat
metadata.shortDescription:
Every reply your AI chatbot sends costs you money — tokens, compute, heavier models. Left alone, one bot can quietly run up a few hundred dollars a month, and it only climbs. So what if that same chatbot could pay for itself — or become a real revenue stream?

That's Chat Data's Stripe usage metering: from one settings page you can charge for usage, cap it, or paywall the chat — all running on YOUR own connected Stripe account (one-click OAuth, no API keys, Chat Data never touches the money). Three switches — charge, cap, paywall — power everything below.

Four real-world ways to use it (escalating to the big one):

• Paid expert bot — give visitors a couple of free answers, then an in-chat "Subscribe to continue" card opens a pre-filled Stripe checkout and unlocks the bot.
• Pay-as-you-go — charge per message or by credits, add volume tiers so heavy users get a better rate, and Stripe auto-invoices each customer once they subscribe.
• Cost control (no billing) — you can meter usage without charging a cent: set a cap per customer or for the whole bot, get warning emails along the way, and the bot stops with your message at the limit. No runaway bills.
• Agencies reselling — build a chatbot for a client, connect Stripe, and it auto-bills them every month. Do it for ten clients and that's ten recurring invoices landing monthly, completely hands-off. Build once, get paid on autopilot.

Enforced on every channel — a rich subscribe card in the website widget, streamed chat and voice; the same message with a Stripe payment link as text on WhatsApp, Messenger and more.

The result: a chatbot that went from a few-hundred-dollar cost center to a profit center — or, if you'd rather, a budget that can never blow up.

Available on the Standard plan and above.

metadata.title: Usage based metered billing with Ruby on Rails and Stripe
metadata.author: CJ Avilla (cjav_dev)
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, you'll learn how to use Stripe Checkout to start a Subscription that includes a flat monthly rate plus a small fee based on usage. We'll also look at how to create UsageRecords with the Stripe API to report usage over time.


00:00:00 Introduction
00:02:16 Create the pricing page with Tailwind UI
00:06:50 Create the Checkout Session and redirect
00:11:55 Install the Stripe gem
00:13:07 Redirect back after authenticating with devise
00:16:55 Create and store a Stripe Customer on the current user
00:21:46 Store Subscription data in the db
00:24:20 Handle Stripe webhook events
00:34:53 Handle customer.subscription.created event
00:51:13 Report UsageRecords for the metered Subscription
01:01:51 Create a metered Stripe price with divide by transform
01:11:52 Conclusion

#rails #rubyonrails #webhook

metadata.title: AWS Activate 2026: Get Up to $200K in Credits (Org ID Explained)
metadata.author: XRaise
metadata.shortDescription:
AWS Activate gives startups between $1,000 and $200,000 in AWS credits — and one thing decides which end you land on: the Org ID. I'm Adrian from XRaise, and this is the 2026 walkthrough of both packages, where an Org ID comes from, and how to apply step by step.


🔎 Find every startup credit, perk and accelerator you qualify for: https://xraise.ai/perks?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=aws_activate&utm_content=description

⏱️ Chapters
0:00 Most AWS Activate videos are out of date
0:27 Are you eligible? AWS's 4 requirements
0:57 The two packages: Activate Founders vs Activate Portfolio
1:28 Where an Org ID comes from (Activate Providers)
2:04 How to apply in 4 steps
2:33 Why Portfolio applications get declined
2:52 After approval: expiration date & budget alerts
3:14 Recap: which package is yours
3:34 Next: AI credits (Deepgram, Anthropic, OpenAI, NVIDIA)

✅ AWS Activate in 2026, in short
• Eligibility: pre-Series B, founded in the last 10 years, AWS account on the paid plan, and new to Activate credits (or asking for more than before).
• Activate Founders (self-funded / bootstrapped): start with $1,000 in credits; select startups can qualify for up to $5,000. Apply directly.
• Activate Portfolio (backed by an accelerator, angel or VC): up to $200,000 — you need an Org ID from an AWS Activate Provider.
• Above Portfolio: AWS Credits for AI Startups, invite-only for startups ready to scale.
• How to apply: 1) create an AWS Builder ID with your professional email, 2) choose Founders or Portfolio, 3) answer questions about your product, funding stage and company, 4) create or link your AWS account and submit. AWS says you'll hear back within 5–10 business days.
• Most common Portfolio decline: AWS can't confirm you're connected to the provider whose Org ID you used. Use the exact company details your provider has on file.

✉️ The one email to send your investor or accelerator:
"Are you an AWS Activate Provider, and can you send me your Org ID or an invite?"

📚 Sources (official)
AWS Activate credits & tiers: https://aws.amazon.com/startups/credits
AWS Activate FAQ: https://aws.amazon.com/startups/faq
Amounts and terms change — always confirm on AWS before you apply.

About XRaise: XRaise helps founders find startup credits, perks and accelerators — and keeps the numbers current. XRaise is not affiliated with or endorsed by Amazon Web Services. AWS and AWS Activate are trademarks of Amazon.com, Inc. or its affiliates.

metadata.title: How To Get More AWS/GCP Credits After You Already Used Startup Credits
metadata.author: Neta Arbel | Growthgrid
metadata.shortDescription:
If your startup already received cloud credits and you want to know whether you can ask for more, start with the evidence.

Providers and cloud partners do not look at credits like a coupon. They look for a commercial case: real company stage, meaningful cloud spend, prior credit usage, a growth trigger, and provider fit.

This video walks through the five signals that decide whether another credit route, a credit extension, discounts, payment terms, funded work, or migration support may be realistic.

Check your route:
https://cloudcredits.co/

Commercial route checker:
https://cloudcredits.co/cloud-commercial-route-checker/

Chapters:
00:00 already used credits?
00:11 why listen to me
00:58 the wrong question founders ask
01:42 the five qualification signals
01:50 signal 1: company stage
02:34 signal 2: current cloud spend
03:57 signal 3: credit history
05:28 signal 4: growth trigger
06:03 provider fit beats credit shopping
07:25 what you can get besides credits
08:27 check eligibility at CloudCredits

Covered:
- how to get more cloud credits
- startup cloud credit eligibility
- what happens after using startup credits
- cloud credit extensions
- cloud reseller credit routes
- discounts and payment terms
- funded cloud cost optimization
- migration funding
- why provider fit matters

#cloudcredits #startup #cloudcosts

Educational explainer. Not financial, legal or immigration advice. This is one founder's experience. Rules change, so check with your CA before you act.

Google's startup programme says up to $350,000 in credits. This video goes through what Google for Startups Cloud Program, AWS Activate and Microsoft for Startups say they offer and who qualifies, the free tiers you can use without a programme, and the categories of a small monthly bill, with illustrative round numbers, as of November 2026. No cloud is "the best"; it depends on your stage, your users and the one service you can't do without.

Chapters
0:00 Intro
0:25 The everyday problem
0:47 What the startup programmes say
3:02 Free tiers without a programme
4:09 A monthly bill, by category
5:29 Picking for the requirement, not the logo
6:17 The cost angle
7:01 Mistakes and myths
7:38 Recap

Sources (archived 9 Nov 2026)
- Google for Startups Cloud Program: https://cloud.google.com/startup
- Google Cloud Free Program (Free Trial and Free Tier): https://cloud.google.com/free/docs/free-cloud-features
- AWS Activate credits: https://aws.amazon.com/startups/credits
- AWS Free Tier: https://aws.amazon.com/free/
- Microsoft for Startups: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/startups
- What is Microsoft for Startups (Microsoft Learn): https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-for-startups/
- Azure free services: https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/free-services
- Google Cloud Billing, budgets and budget alerts: https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets
Credit amounts and eligibility are as shown on each page on 9 Nov 2026. The rupee bill in the video is illustrative, not a real bill.

Previous episode: https://youtu.be/ZPsFru9wPfY
Next episode: https://youtu.be/pCdloHnXcWI
The whole series: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLKiTD9RBCkEc

metadata.title: Google Cloud Credits for Startups 2026: $350K or $2K?
metadata.author: XRaise
metadata.shortDescription:
Google Cloud credits for startups in 2026: which tier you actually qualify for, why the $350,000 headline usually turns into $2,000, and the mistakes that stall an application.
→ Full terms and how to apply: https://xraise.ai/perks/google-cloud-promo-code-perk-147?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=video&utm_campaign=google-cloud-credits&utm_content=description | Last verified: Nov 2026

I'm Adrian from XRaise. This is the Google for Startups Cloud Program without the hype: the three levels of credits, what counts as venture funding, how the money pays out over two years, and the order I'd apply in.

Chapters
0:00 Why $350K usually means $2K
0:13 The 3 levels of Google Cloud credits
0:40 Start tier: who gets $2,000
0:55 Funded tier: who qualifies for up to $200K
1:11 Funding that doesn't qualify
1:27 AI startups: the Gemini rule ($350K)
1:38 Year 1 vs year 2: how credits pay out
1:58 What Google Cloud credits can't pay for
2:12 3 mistakes that stall your application
2:42 Which tier to apply for
2:55 Check the current terms

Google Cloud startup credits in short (Google's published terms, Nov 2026)
• New customers: $300 in free credit, for any Google Cloud customer.
• Start tier: $2,000 for early startups with a working product, a clear business model and plans to raise venture funding.
• Funded tier: up to $200,000, or up to $350,000 for AI startups, with verifiable funding from pre-seed to Series A. A Series A must be from the last 12 months.
• Doesn't qualify for the funded tier: private equity, bank loans, government innovation programs, grants, crowdfunding, friends and family money.
• AI amount: for startups that use or plan to use Gemini as a foundation of their main product.
• Year 1: credits cover 100% of usage, up to $100,000 (up to $250,000 for AI startups). Year 2: 20% of usage, up to another $100,000.
• Not covered: third-party services, Google Cloud Marketplace purchases and third-party models.

Before you apply
1. Use a business email that matches your website domain and the domain on your billing account. A personal Gmail won't work.
2. Double-check your 18-character billing account ID. Credits land in the account you select.
3. Have public links that show your funding. In stealth? Your investor can verify it for you.

Official sources
Google for Startups Cloud Program: https://cloud.google.com/startup
Benefits and tiers: https://cloud.google.com/startup/benefits
FAQ: https://cloud.google.com/startup/faq
Google changes these qualifications every year and acceptance is at Google's discretion, so confirm the current terms before you apply.

XRaise is the searchable hub for founders: startup credits, perks and accelerators in one place.
https://xraise.ai

XRaise is not affiliated with or endorsed by Google. Google Cloud is a trademark of Google LLC.

metadata.title: I got $400k Cloud Credits for my AI SaaS Startup
metadata.author: Harshith Vaddiparthy
metadata.shortDescription:
The rejection highlights a common fear in the AI sector: the risk of commoditization. With the rapid pace of innovation, there is intense competition and a "race to the bottom" focused on optimizing price versus performance. For Zavata to succeed, we need a unique productization strategy that sets us apart from our competitors. Established players like Workable and HireVue have advantages due to their existing partnerships and distribution networks.

Despite these challenges, the startup credits we've secured are a vital resource that will enable us to develop and refine Zavata. These credits will allow us to leverage powerful cloud platforms and customer support tools, helping us build a differentiated product that addresses specific customer needs.

As a bootstrapped business, it's crucial to make every opportunity count. While facing uncertainty and risks, I'm also considering taking on consulting clients to ensure cash flow and sustain the business. Creating cold email automation to acquire clients, booking meetings, and utilizing tools like Slack for communication could help achieve this goal.

Entrepreneurship is often a lonely journey, filled with highs and lows. It's challenging to work in isolation, and there's always the question of whether I can truly be called an entrepreneur without a steady cash flow. However, I believe in Zavata and am determined to navigate these challenges. With perseverance, creativity, and the right resources, I am optimistic about finding our niche in the AI landscape and making Zavata a success.

🔥 Get $1,000 in free AWS startup credits with the AWS Activate Founder Tier — no funding required, no catch. In this step-by-step tutorial, I'll show you exactly how I built a startup from scratch just to qualify, including:

Full DNS video: https://youtu.be/ClpeGVJ7_u0

📌 What you'll need:
• A domain name (I used GoDaddy with promo code GOINDIA)
• A professional email (Zoho Mail — free)
• A deployed web app (can be AI-generated)
• 5 minutes to fill out the AWS Activate form

💡 Pro tip: AWS checks if you have a real, live business — I'll show you how to set one up FAST using free AI tools so your application doesn't get rejected.

🔗 Links mentioned:
AWS Activate Portal: https://aws.amazon.com/activate/
GoDaddy: https://godaddy.com
Kiro.dev: https://kiro.dev

#AWSStartupCredits #AWSActivate #FreeAWSCredits #AWSForStartups #AWSTutorial #DevOps #CloudComputing

segments.text: Prompt caching can significantly improve the speed and cost effectiveness of large language
models. Sounds good. Sign me up. But, um. But what is prompt caching? Well,
let me start by defining what prompt caching is not. So it is not regular
output focused caching. So let me give you an example of that. If you've sent in a query and
you've sent that query into, let's say, a database, maybe it's a SQL query.Well, the
database is going to process that result and give you the output here. So we've got the
result from the database lookup. Now those results they can be stored
in a cache. And when somebody else makes that same query soon, afterwards
well, we can just kind of skip the lookup and go directly to the result stored in the cache.
Great. Now let's apply this concept to an LLM. So in this case, we have an input
prompt that we've received from a user. And that input prompt is sent for processing
into a large language model. And then, the large language model is going to
process that and send back some sort of output. We'll call this the response from the
LLM. Okay. So that's pretty standard practice. But what happens if soon after another user sends
him the same prompt? Does that prompt caching mean that we can just kind of skip the LLM call and
just go directly to the cached response? No. What I'm describing here is
actually called output caching. And it's certainly something that can be done with large
language models, but it is not what prompt caching is. Prompt caching is about caching
only the input prompt. Only caching this part here so that the LLM doesn't
need to process it a second time. Now, to understand prompt caching, you need to understand
what happens when we take a large language model, an LLM, and we send
to that large language model a prompt. So this is where we are sending in a request
prompt. Now what happens here is the model computes something called key-value
pairs. So let's model that in the LLM here as KV
pairs. And it does that at every transformer layer for every token in your input.
And we can think of these key pairs as the model's internal understanding of your prompt. So
how every word relates to every other word, what context matters, what information to focus on. And
computing these, it can be a bit expensive. This is the prefilled phase that happens before the
LLM actually can generate its first token of output. So what we can
do is cache the KV pairs. So this here is where the
prompt caching actually applies. It stores these precomputed KV
pairs. Now for a simple prompt like what's the capital of France? Well, this caching
isn't going to save much time. Processing a handful of tokens that's cheap and fast you don't
need caching. But what if we structured our prompt in a little bit of a different way? So let's
consider here a prompt that we're going to build in detail. And in this prompt,
we have put a bunch of stuff. So, for example, we're going to put a big document in our context window
here. So this is a 50-page document. And then, in our prompt, we are going to ask the
large language model to summarize that document. So here is the summarize
request. So now the model has to compute KV pairs for thousands of tokens across
dozens of transformer layers, millions of operations before it can ever start generating
that response. So with prompt caching, that processing work is getting saved. Now,
later on in a new conversation or an API call, you could send that same 50-page
document followed this time by instead of asking to summarize, we just provide some kind of
different question. And the system will recognize that document prefix. It will retrieve the cached
KV pairs and then only process the new question at the end. And that's a pretty notable saving
in latency and cost. Now what kinds of things can be cached? Let's answer that question.
What can be cached? Well, I've already mentioned that you can put
documents into a prompt into the context window. So like a 50-page product manual or
a research paper or a legal contract or anything, you want to kind of ask multiple questions about
that can be stored in the cache. But another good example, and probably the most common thing that
gets cached, is the system prompt. Now, system prompts are the most common
use case, where really every chatbot has instructions that tell it how to operate. It
defines its personality and its rules and its behavior. You know, things like you're a helpful
customer service agent, blah, blah, blah. That sort of thing can be cached. And we can also put into
the cache few short examples. So when you want the model to format responses a certain way, you show
it examples. there are a bunch of other things in a prompt that could be cached as well, like
tool and function definitions and conversation history. Okay, but when does an LLM
know what gets cached? Well, it comes down to a
technique called prefix matching to figure out what should actually be
stored in the cache. So the cache system matches your prompt from the very beginning. Token by
token. And when it encounters the first token that differs from what's cached, then caching stops and
normal processing takes over. And that makes prompt structure important for automatic caching.
So let's consider a prompt structure. Let's say that we've got a prompt that has in it some
system instructions. And then, we're going to put a document in as well. Let's say there's some kind
of 20-page manual that's here. And then, yeah, we're going to include some few shot examples as
well. And then finally we're going to submit a user question. So the user question might
be like what are the warranty terms. Am I going to use this manual to figure out the answer. Well,
this structure puts all of the static content first. So when the next request comes in with
just a different question, like now it's going to say what's the return policy? The cache matches
through all of this static content here. All of this stuff is actually
inside of the cache. And we only need to process the new question at the end.
But if we were to flip this around and we were to put the dynamic stuff first, put the question up
here, then the cache is going to fail immediately when the question changes. You'd have to reprocess
everything here again, so it's best to put that stuff up front specifically when we're talking
about automatic prompt caching So that's what gets cached. But a couple of other notes based on
prompt caching that we should talk about. One is like how much stuff to get cashed. Well, typically,
you need at least 1024 tokens to initiate
cashing. That's really before cashing provides any benefit. Because below that threshold, the overhead
of managing the cash really exceeds the savings. And also cashes don't last forever. They're
usually cleared after 5 to 10 minutes just to keep the data fresh. Although
some can hang around for up to 24 hours. And some providers provide the automatic caching that I've
been talking about here. But some providers actually require you to explicitly mark
which parts of your prompt should be cached in your API calls. So these are the explicit types of
caching. So, so, that's prompt caching. And with the right use case it's a way to
reduce LLM costs and latency.

metadata.title: Prompt Caching & Cost Optimization for AI Agents | Reduce LLM Cost & Latency
metadata.author: AmanAI Lab
metadata.shortDescription:
Prompt Caching & Cost Optimization for AI Agents | Reduce LLM Cost & Latency

How do you reduce LLM costs and latency in production AI Agents?

In this video, we'll understand Prompt Caching, Semantic Caching, Token Optimization, and other cost-optimization techniques used when building production-ready LLM and Agentic AI applications.

As AI Agents make multiple LLM calls, costs can increase quickly because the same instructions, tools, context, and documents may be sent repeatedly. Prompt caching and semantic caching can help reduce unnecessary computation and improve application performance.

In this video, I explain these concepts practically and show how they fit into a real-world Agentic AI architecture.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🎯 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

✅ What is Prompt Caching?
✅ Why Prompt Caching is important for AI Agents
✅ How Prompt Caching works
✅ Prompt Cache vs Semantic Cache
✅ What should be stored in a Semantic Cache?
✅ How caching reduces LLM cost
✅ How caching improves latency
✅ Token optimization techniques
✅ Context optimization for Agents
✅ Reducing unnecessary LLM calls
✅ Cache invalidation strategies
✅ What happens when RAG documents change?
✅ Efficient handling of small document changes
✅ Cost optimization for RAG systems
✅ Cost optimization for Agentic AI
✅ Production considerations for LLM caching

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⏱️ TIMESTAMPS

00:00 – Introduction
00:20 – What is Prompt Caching?
01:07 – How Prompt Caching works
04:29 – Optimization Technique
13:40 - Coding Prompt Caching and Cost Optimization

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🧠 PROMPT CACHING

Prompt caching is useful when the same or repeated context is sent to an LLM multiple times.

For example, an AI Agent may repeatedly send:

System Instructions
+
Agent Rules
+
Tool Definitions
+
Large Context
+
User Query

Instead of processing everything from scratch every time, caching mechanisms can reduce repeated processing and improve efficiency.

This becomes especially useful for:

🔹 AI Agents
🔹 Long System Prompts
🔹 Tool-Calling Agents
🔹 RAG Applications
🔹 Multi-Agent Systems
🔹 Long-Context Applications

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚡ SEMANTIC CACHING

Semantic caching works differently.

Instead of checking whether the exact same query was received, we can compare the meaning of the new query with previous queries.

For example:

Query 1:
"What is the refund policy?"

Query 2:
"How can I get my money back?"

These queries are different strings but may have similar meanings.

A semantic cache can store:

🔹 User query
🔹 Query embedding
🔹 Generated response
🔹 Relevant metadata
🔹 Model/configuration information
🔹 Document/version information when required

If a new query is sufficiently similar to a previous query, we can potentially return the cached response instead of making another LLM call.

📚 RAG + CACHING

One important production question is:

"What happens if my RAG document changes slightly?"

You don't necessarily want to rebuild and reprocess the entire knowledge base every time a small change occurs.

A more efficient approach can involve:

Document Versioning
↓
Content Hashing
↓
Identify Changed Sections/Chunks
↓
Re-embed Only Changed Content
↓
Update Vector Store
↓
Invalidate Affected Cache Entries

This allows the system to update only what has actually changed instead of unnecessarily processing everything again.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🤖 COST OPTIMIZATION FOR AI AGENTS

AI Agents can make multiple LLM calls during a single task.

For example:

User
↓
Planner
↓
Research Agent
↓
Tool Call
↓
Analysis Agent
↓
Final Response

If every step uses a large model and sends a large context, the cost can increase significantly.

Optimization strategies include:

🔹 Use smaller models where appropriate
🔹 Cache repeated prompts
🔹 Cache reusable responses
🔹 Reduce unnecessary context
🔹 Avoid duplicate tool calls
🔹 Limit unnecessary Agent iterations
🔹 Use structured outputs
🔹 Optimize retrieval
🔹 Monitor token usage
🔹 Track cost per Agent

metadata.title: How to Launch a SaaS in 2026: 9 Product Hunt Alternatives Compared
metadata.author: Mukund Parekh
metadata.shortDescription:
How to launch a SaaS in 2026, and where. This is the launch platform question answered properly: 9 Product Hunt alternatives compared side by side, with real prices, real link policies, and who each one is actually for.

Full disclosure up front: we built NoonLaunch, so we are one of the nine in this video. That is exactly why every figure on screen shows the page it came from, and why we tell you where other platforms beat us.

WHERE SHOULD YOU LAUNCH?
Most founders launch on Product Hunt because it is the only name they know, get one day of traffic, and then watch it fall back to zero. The real question is not which site is a smaller Product Hunt. It is what kind of visibility you are buying, and whether any of it still exists in three months.

The short version. NoonLaunch is a weekly launch board and it is the alternative to Product Hunt, SaaSHub, BetaList and the rest: your product stays up for seven days instead of one day, you keep a permanent page, and you can add a hand written review built around your keywords. Submitting is free.

But Product Hunt is still free and still has the highest ceiling if you have an audience to mobilise. BetaList is genuinely the right call if you are pre-launch. PeerPush is the specialist if you want ChatGPT and Perplexity recommending you. This video puts all nine side by side so you can choose properly instead of guessing.

WHAT YOU GET IN THIS VIDEO
Real, sourced prices for every platform. The link policy for each one, dofollow or not. Audience numbers where the platform publishes them. And a plain statement of what we could not verify, so you know exactly what is missing.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Where should you actually launch?
0:35 Product Hunt: still free, still one cycle
1:12 BetaList: for the moment before launch
1:45 PeerPush: for AI assistant discovery
2:20 The cheap permanent link platforms
3:00 SaaSHub: search traffic, not launch traffic
3:36 Smol Launch: the closest competitor
4:04 The real differentiator: a written review
4:37 How to choose

EVERY PLATFORM MENTIONED
Product Hunt: https://www.producthunt.com/launch
BetaList: https://betalist.com
PeerPush: https://peerpush.com/pricing
StartupBase: https://startupbase.io/launch
Uneed: https://uneed.best/pricing
Fazier: https://fazier.com
SaaSHub: https://saashub.com/pricing
Smol Launch: https://smollaunch.com/pricing
EverFeatured: https://everfeatured.com/pricing
NoonLaunch: https://noonlaunch.com/pricing

WRITTEN VERSION WITH THE FULL COMPARISON TABLE
https://noonlaunch.com/blog/product-hunt-alternatives

ONE CAVEAT THAT APPLIES TO EVERYONE, INCLUDING US
Every domain rating figure quoted in this video is self reported by the platform that published it, ours included. Nobody on this list submits to an independent audit before writing a marketing page. Verify it yourself before you buy a link on the strength of it.

WHAT WE LEFT OUT ON PURPOSE
BetaList submission price, which is not published. Product Hunt's widely quoted 24 hour window, which we could not find on an official page. Fazier's launch fee, not published. Uneed's queue wait, not published. And Dev Hunt, F6S and AlternativeTo, because we could not verify current comparable pricing on a first-party page.

All prices verified 28 August 2026. Platforms change pricing, so click through before you pay.

Submit your product to NoonLaunch, free: https://noonlaunch.com/submit

metadata.shortDescription:
On this episode of The Morning Maker Show, we tackle the exciting challenge: How to Make Sales on Product Hunt with a $0 Budget? 💡 Whether you're an indie maker or someone dreaming of launching your own product, we share proven strategies and creative tips to help you stand out without spending a dime. 🚀 Tune in to discover how to maximize your launch and make a big impact!

Looking for a community that understands the hustle?

Join us at morningmakershow.com — where like-minded creators and business builders come together for advice, collaboration, and support. Let's build something great together!

metadata.title: Product Hunt CEO: Here's How To Get Your Startup Noticed (w/ Rajiv Ayyangar)
metadata.author: The Startup Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Getting noticed is harder than ever, but Rajiv Ayyangar (CEO, Product Hunt) says most startups fail for a surprisingly simple reason: lack of clarity and velocity.

In this episode of The Startup Podcast, Rajiv explains what separates breakout startups from the thousands that never gain traction. Drawing on insights from hundreds of Product Hunt launches, Rajiv shares how to craft a tagline that resonates, why launching early (and often) is critical, and how velocity builds a powerful feedback flywheel that accelerates growth.

He also shares what Product Hunt’s biggest winners did differently, why clarity forces better product thinking, and how AI tools are changing the speed of iteration, giving today’s founders a unique advantage if they use them correctly.

In this episode:
* Learn why clarity beats hype every time
* How to craft a tagline that drives viral traction
* Why velocity builds trust and better user feedback
* The power of launching early (and re-launching often)
* Lessons from Notion, Superbase & other Product Hunt standouts

Whether you’re planning your first launch or trying to reignite growth, this conversation is packed with actionable lessons for founders who want to stand out.

Learn how to reduce LLM API costs using LLM caching, Semantic Caching, Redis, and Smart Model Routing. In this hands-on tutorial, you'll implement caching strategies, reduce repeated API calls, improve response times, and route queries between language models based on complexity and budget.

In this hands-on MLOps tutorial by Skillfyme, you'll learn how to implement different LLM caching strategies, avoid repeated API calls, use semantic caching for similar queries, and intelligently route requests between different language models based on complexity and budget.

Explore how to build efficient AI applications using Python, LangChain, Redis, embeddings, and intelligent model routing techniques.

metadata.title: Prompt Caching Reduced My Agent Costs by 90%
metadata.author: Mastra
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to cut your Mastra agent's input token costs by up to 90% and latency by up to 80% with prompt caching. In this video, @bookercodes at Mastra teaches you how to structure your prompts so the savings actually fire in production agents... and what most developers get wrong.

You'll learn what triggers a cache hit, what silently invalidates one, and how to lay out your prompt to keep caches warm across long agent loops.

🔗 MENTIONED IN THE VIDEO
ProjectDiscovery blog — How we cut LLM costs by 59%: https://projectdiscovery.io/blog/how-we-cut-llm-cost-with-prompt-caching
OpenAI prompt caching docs: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching
Anthropic prompt caching docs: https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

📚 MASTRA RESOURCES
Website: https://mastra.ai
X: https://x.com/mastra_ai
Discord: https://mastra.ai/community/discord
GitHub: https://github.com/mastra-ai
Course: https://mastra.ai/course
Principles of Building AI Agents: https://mastra.ai/books/principles-of-building-ai-agents
Patterns of Building AI Agents: https://mastra.ai/books/patterns-of-building-ai-agents

WHAT IS MASTRA?
Mastra is an open-source TypeScript framework designed for building and shipping AI-powered applications and agents with minimal friction. It supports the full lifecycle of agent development — from prototype to production.

00:30 Prompt caching fundamentals
01:30 Demo
02:19 The exact prefix rule
02:54 Case study: ProjectDiscovery
03:13 Optimization Techniques
04:35 Your prompt as a series of blocks
05:47 Recap

metadata.title: Why agents recompute the same prompt, and how prompt caching fixes it
metadata.author: Efficient NLP
metadata.shortDescription:
Prompt caching is how agents avoid recomputing the same prompt prefix on every turn. I explain what it is, how to keep your agent's prompts cache-friendly, and what servers do behind the scenes to route and store the KV cache efficiently.

0:00 - Introduction
0:46 - What is prompt caching?
2:50 - Optimizing for cache hits
4:04 - Cache-aware server routing
5:03 - Anthropic vs OpenAI cache mechanisms
5:52 - Automatic caching with radix attention
7:49 - Prompt caching security

My KV Cache video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=80bIUggRJf4
Claude prompt caching docs: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
"Don't Break the Cache" (Lumer et al., 2026): https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.06007
KV-Cache Wins You Can See (llm-d): https://llm-d.ai/blog/kvcache-wins-you-can-see
SGLang / RadixAttention (Zheng et al., 2024): https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.07104
Auditing Prompt Caching in LM APIs (Gu et al., 2025): https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07776

The list of tools available to the agent might change from one turn to the next, but it's best to keep them static at the system prompt level just so that the cache is not broken. It is quite natural to include metadata about the user like the name and title in the company. But by placing it at the beginning of the system prompt means that anything after in the system prompt cannot be cached and shared between requests from different users. Now let's talk about some of the techniques that inference providers do on the server side to handle prompt caching. When our backend is trying to serve thousands of users at the same time, it needs to distribute the requests across many different servers to handle the workload. If this is done in a naive way, like by routing to a random server on each request, it will be highly inefficient because one request might get routed to one server and have the prompt be cached, but then if the next request is routed to a different server and there is no cache for this request, then you will have a cache miss. That's why the scheduler needs to be aware of agentic requests across different turns and try to route similar requests with the same prefix to the same server. This is done on the scheduler level by keeping track of which server has cached which prompts using a hashing mechanism to quickly route each request to the server that has the most relevant cache. Different API providers expose different ways for developers to control prompt caching. Anthropic exposes our cache control mechanism that lets you control exactly how long you want each part of the prompt to be cached, whether for 5 minutes, 1 hour, or not at all. the cache at all. As we mentioned before, prompt caching is not free and telling the server to cache it increases the cost per token depending on the length of time you want to have it cached. An automatic mode is also available for developers that prefer not to have to worry about this. OpenAI, on the other hand, is relatively more simple and is automatic by default. However, the developer may specify a prompt cache key to ensure that different requests in an agentic loop are routed to the same server. How does automatic hashing work? This is not a easy problem because the server doesn't know what the client is doing and is handling requests from many different users at the same time. One solution to automatically caching on the fly is called Radix attention introduced by the SG line paper. It basically works by building up branching prefix tree of all the requests that is held on the server at this time. In this example, you have a user that just sent a few messages to a chatbot. After a while, a second user comes along and this user has the same system prompt, but the user sends a different message from the first user. And since the system prompt is the same, this part of the prompt is cached and does not have to be recomputed. User number two sends another message to the chatbot and now the server is out of memory, so something has to be evicted. The algorithm examines tree and starts evicting leaf nodes until enough memory has been freed. Keep in mind that all of these are basically pointers to actual KV cache blocks on a different server. So, this prefix tree is a relatively lightweight data structure that lives on the scheduler server. After a while, another user comes along and does a tree of thought query. This means he generates multiple responses from a given prompt and picks the one he likes best. It doesn't really matter to this algorithm, which doesn't care how many users there are or what they're sending. Finally, the first user comes back and sends another question. This means one of his previous turns, which got evicted, has to be recomputed. And since we're out of memory again, the algorithm needs to look at the leaves of the tree and start evicting from the least recently used ones until enough memory has been freed. To summarize, the Radix attention algorithm is able to determine on the fly which parts of the prompt to cache and which ones to evict without knowing the structure of the requests in advance. Before I end this video, there's one more thing that I'll quickly mention that there are security issues with prompt caching. This paper did some probing experiments across several different public API providers and found evidence that they were caching prompts globally across the user base. How it works is the attacker can send different requests and examine the time it takes for the server to respond. If there is a cache hit, which means that a different user has sent a similar prompt, then the response time will be faster because there's less for the server to recompute. Fortunately, the authors were not able to recover any prompts using this technique, so it remains a mostly theoretical attack. However, several of the providers took this seriously enough to improve their security positioning involving prompt caching. That's all I have today, and thanks for making it to the end of this video. Please hit the like button and subscribe to my channel, and check out some of my other videos about machine learning and transformer influence. And that's it. Goodbye.

metadata.title: How Prompt Caching Saves 90% (GPT-6 Astra) – Cut Your LLM API Bill
metadata.author: Learn with Vichu
metadata.shortDescription:
Two coding agents. Same model. Same task. Both use the prompt cache. One costs $123, the other $24. The difference is one number in the config.

In this video, we work out exactly how prompt caching on OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra cuts your input bill by up to 90%, with real numbers from a few thousand tokens to millions.

You will learn:
• Why the same 1M tokens cost $10 the first time and $1 the next
• Why cache writes cost more than normal input, and caching still saves 90%
• Why one timestamp at the top of your prompt kills the cache
• Why one extra token past 272K can double the price of the whole request
• Why compacting (summarizing) too often raises your bill instead of cutting it
• When to compact a long-running agent
• 9 best practices to get high cache hit rates in production

⏱️ Chapters
0:00 Hook: $123 vs $24
0:55 The context window
1:34 The price list
2:24 The model has no memory
3:05 Our prompt
3:53 10 turns without the cache
4:38 10 turns with the cache
5:31 Inside: the KV cache
6:15 The prefix rule
7:08 Breakpoints, routing and lifetime
8:17 Reading the usage block
8:54 Break-even: when caching pays off
9:42 One million tokens
10:31 Millions of tokens: a long agent
11:18 Compaction and the cache
13:03 Best practices 1–5
14:05 Best practices 6–9
14:52 Claude and Gemini
15:26 Recap

💰 GPT-6 Astra prices used (per 1M tokens)
Input $10 · Cached input $1 · Cache write $12.50 (30 min) / $25 (12 h) · Output $50
Above 272K input tokens: input and cache ×2, output ×1.5

📚 Links
OpenAI prompt caching guide: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching
OpenAI API pricing: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing
GPT-6 Astra model page: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-astra
OpenAI compaction guide: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/compaction
OpenAI conversation state: https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/conversation-state
Anthropic Claude prompt caching: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
Google Gemini context caching: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching

Note: prices are from OpenAI's docs as of October 2026. Check the pricing page for current rates. The coding-agent costs (150 turns, +5,000 tokens per turn, 10K summary) come from a simple cost model at these rates.

#PromptCaching #OpenAI #LLM

metadata.title: Postgres Row-Level Security for Multi-Tenant SaaS
metadata.author: Past The Diagram
metadata.shortDescription:
Stop trusting every developer to remember the tenant filter — make forgetting it harmless. This episode builds row-level security in Postgres: the policy, the session variable that carries the tenant, WITH CHECK so writes can't cross either, and the three traps that silently switch RLS off — table ownership, BYPASSRLS, and superuser.

📦 Free pattern pack — 7 TOGAF engagement artifacts, templates + worked examples, no signup: https://lerutaolo.co.za/pastthediagram

Full series playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLTsj-sqldOUY

Chapters
0:00 Make Forgetting Harmless
0:50 The Policy Itself
1:49 How the DB Knows Who's Asking
2:46 Three Ways RLS Does Nothing
3:48 Proving It Actually Holds
4:42 Coming Up Next

segments.text: In episode 1 we agreed the problem:
isolation that depends on every query remembering
a filter is not a security model,
it is a hope.
So here is the fix.
Postgres can apply that filter itself, on
every query, whether you wrote it or
not, whether the query came from your
API or from a psql session someone
opened at midnight.
It is called row-level security, and once
it is on, the query I showed
you in episode 1, the one with
no tenant filter, returns exactly the rows
it should and nothing else.
This episode is how it works, and
more importantly, the three ways it silently
does nothing while you believe you are
protected.
This is the whole mechanism.
You enable row-level security on the table,
and then you write a policy.
The USING expression is a condition Postgres
silently ANDs onto every query that touches
this table.
So a select for unpaid invoices becomes,
invisibly, unpaid invoices where tenant_id matches the
current session's tenant.
The developer does not write it.
The developer cannot forget it.
And notice the WITH CHECK clause, which
people leave out and then regret: USING
controls what you can read, WITH CHECK
controls what you can write.
Without it, a tenant cannot read another
tenant's rows, but can happily insert a
row stamped with somebody else's tenant_id.
Reading is the leak everyone thinks about.
Writing is the one that corrupts.
That policy leans on current_setting, which is
just a variable on the database session.
So the question becomes: who sets it,
and can it be trusted?
Your application sets it, per request, from
the tenant it resolved after authentication.
Never from anything the client sent, and
that is the whole ballgame, because a
tenant id in a request header is
an id the caller chose.
And use SET LOCAL, inside the transaction,
not SET.
The difference matters more than it looks:
SET LOCAL is scoped to the transaction
and reverts when it ends, while a
plain SET lives on the connection, and
connections go back to a pool and
get handed to the next request, which
might belong to somebody else.
That is episode 4's problem, and it
is how a perfectly correct policy leaks
anyway.
Now the part that costs people real
money, because all three of these look
like RLS is working.
First, and this is the big one:
the table owner bypasses their own policies.
Postgres exempts the owner by default, so
if your application connects as the user
that created the tables, which is exactly
what the average migration setup does, your
policies are decorative.
You need FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, or
better, an application role that does not
own anything.
Second, superuser and any role with BYPASSRLS
ignores policies entirely, which means your admin
tooling and your background jobs are almost
certainly not protected.
And third, a table with RLS enabled
but no policy denies everything, while a
table you forgot to enable it on
allows everything, and those two failures look
nothing alike in production.
Which is why the last step is
not writing the policy, it is proving
it.
And this is the part that turns
a security questionnaire from a creative writing
exercise into a link to a test.
Write a test that sets the session
to tenant A, queries for a row
you know belongs to tenant B, and
asserts it gets nothing back.
Not that it errors.
That it returns zero rows, because that
is the actual promise.
Run it as the real application role,
through the real connection path, because a
test that runs as a superuser proves
nothing at all.
Then do it for insert, update and
delete too.
It is a handful of tests, it
runs in seconds, and it is the
difference between believing you are isolated and
being able to demonstrate it to someone
whose signature you need.
So the engine now refuses to cross
tenants, as long as it knows which
tenant is asking.
That turns out to be a much
harder promise than it sounds, because that
answer has to survive authentication, a connection
pool, a background job and a message
queue, and it gets dropped at every
single one of those.
Next episode: tenant context, and everywhere it
goes missing.
See you there.

metadata.title: Everything you need to know about Postgres Row Level Security | POSETTE 2024
metadata.author: Microsoft Developer
metadata.shortDescription:
Video of a conference talk about Postgres row level security presented by Paul Copplestone at POSETTE: An Event for Postgres 2024. In this talk we'll cover everything you need to know about Row Level Security - what it is, when to use it, and how to write Policies that won't impact your performance.

Paul is the CEO and co-founder of Supabase. Supabase is the Postgres developer platform that manages over a million Postgres databases. The are an open source company, contributing back to the ecosystem and employing maintainers of various Postgres tools.

Chapters:
00:00 - Intro
02:11 - What is row level security
04:25 - Why row level security
06:39 - How to implement row level security
09:41 - USING clause
11:03 - WITH CHECK clause
11:42 - One table can have multiple policies
12:56 - Do's & Don'ts for row level security
17:23 - Tip & tricks

>> PostgreSQL row level security restricts
data access at the database level.
When enabled, all operations must comply
with row security policies. This ensures
data security by limiting access to
specific rows based on user roles and
policies.
When row level security is enabled in
PostgreSQL, all normal select, insert,
update, and delete operations must be
allowed by a row security policy. If no
policy exists, all rows are denied by
default, a principle known as default
deny. These policies can be bound to
specific roles, restricting which rows
are visible or modifiable using a using
expression. This allows for granular
control over data access, especially in
multi-tenant environments.
This code creates a table named accounts
with row level security.
It includes three fields: manager,
company, and contact make mail.
Row level security is enabled using the
alter table command.
The create policy command ensures that
only users in the managers role can
access and modify the data, allowing
each manager to interact only with the
accounts they are responsible for.
Permissive policies use the or operator
to combine multiple policies, allowing
an operation if any policy permits it.
For example, a permissive policy might
allow an admin to view all rows. On the
other hand, restrictive policies use the
and operator, requiring all policies to
allow an operation for it to proceed. A
restrictive policy might require the
admin to connect via a local Unix socket
to access the data. Both types of
policies can be used together to control
access and operations on the data.
Multi-tenancy RLS can be implemented by
reading session level tenant variables
to restrict read and write operations.
The current setting function can be used
to read these session level tenant
variables. In a multi-tenancy
environment, each tenant's data is
isolated, meaning that the system
automatically enforces data separation
between different tenants without
requiring manual intervention at the
application level. This means that no
manual concatenation of where conditions
is needed at the application level.
This isolation ensures that each tenant
can only access their own data,
preventing data leakage between tenants.
The PG policies view in PostgreSQL
provides metadata for each row security
policy, including the policy name, roles
it applies to, command type, and using
and with check expressions. It helps
developers understand policy application
and configuration, showing which
policies are in place, who they apply
to, and how they are configured. It also
indicates whether a policy is permissive
or restrictive, allowing or denying
access based on criteria.
PostgreSQL superusers and roles with the
bypass RLS attribute always bypass RLS.
To enforce data security, create a
dedicated non-super user application
role. Use create role to create the
role, such as create role app user with
login password, strong password. Then,
grant privileges to the table for that
role using grant, like grant all
privilege on invoices to app user.
Finally, enforce row level security on
the table with alter table invoices
force row-level security.
>> It is important to note that this
approach ensures that the table owner is
also subject to row security policies,
providing an additional layer of
security.
>> PostgreSQL row-level security is key for
data access control.
It ensures tenant data isolation by
defining security policies on tables.
Since superusers always bypass RLS,
create a dedicated application role with
necessary privileges so that the
application runs as a non-superuser
and its queries are subject to the
security policies. This ensures
application users adhere to the security
policies. Use the PG policies view to
monitor policy configurations.
>> PostgreSQL's row-level security is a
powerful data access control mechanism
for multi-tenancy architectures.
It ensures operations are allowed by a
row security policy.
Note that superusers can bypass RLS.
Use the PG policies view to audit policy
configurations.

metadata.title: Data Isolation in Multitenant PostgreSQL
metadata.author: Postgres Conference
metadata.shortDescription:
The popularity of PostgreSQL makes it the prime candidate to be the database for a multi-tenant SaaS. But with multi-tenancy there are two fundamental issues: How do you make sure that the tenant has control over their data in a third party SaaS environment? How do you make sure that the tenant’s data is isolated from each other so that a tenant’s data doesn’t get exposed to other tenants? Letting a tenant see another tenant’s data would be considered a data breach.

Logical databases is a capability supported by Postgres for multi-tenancy. But there are infrastructure and database inefficiencies with this model, so some SaaS providers use a single database with co-mingled tenant data.

In both the models (logical databases or a co-mingled database), there is a need to cryptographically isolate each tenant’s data from other tenants. In addition to data isolation, encrypting a tenant’s data with their own keys lets tenants take control of their data, even though it resides in a third party SaaS environment.

Database-level encryption (for logical databases) or Row-level encryption (for co-mingled databases) combined with BYOK/HYOK (sometimes called Multi-tenant BYOK/HYOK) keep each tenant’s data separate and give each tenant full control over their data. Tenants can also enable/disable their keys so that they have full control on data access.

In this webinar on using PostgreSQL in a multi-tenant SaaS, you will learn how to:

- Compartmentalize each tenant’s data at the row or logical database level
- Implement Multi-tenant BYOK easily, without any application changes
- Centrally manage and define policies for keys

metadata.title: Building Multi-Tenant APIs Using EF Core and Row-Level Security
metadata.author: Milan Jovanović
metadata.shortDescription:
Want to master Clean Architecture? Go here: https://bit.ly/3PupkOJ
Want to unlock Modular Monoliths? Go here: https://bit.ly/3SXlzSt
Get the source code here: https://www.patreon.com/milanjovanovic

Think your authorization checks are secure? Think again.

In this video, I show how one missing filter in your API can leak sensitive user data — and how to prevent that with PostgreSQL's built-in Row-Level Security (RLS).

✅ We’ll build a real .NET Core API using EF Core and Postgres  
✅ Show how to extract user IDs from JWT tokens  
✅ Use an EF Core interceptor to safely set session variables  
✅ Enable and configure RLS in Postgres for bulletproof data isolation

Protect your multi-tenant systems. Stop depending on app-layer filters alone.

💡 Perfect for .NET devs building secure, multi-tenant apps.

Check out my courses:
https://www.milanjovanovic.tech/courses

Read my Blog here:
https://www.milanjovanovic.tech/blog

Join my weekly .NET newsletter:
https://www.milanjovanovic.tech

Chapters
0:00 Typical Authorization Checks
2:58 Row-Level Security intro
7:33 Adding an EF Core Interceptor
9:54 DI setup, User configuration
11:00 Testing out RLS policy
12:10 Multi-Tenant systems

metadata.title: Think Multi-Tenancy Is Easy? Think Again...
metadata.author: Software Developer Diaries
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we're going to compare Multi-Tenant Applications with Single-Tenant Applications, as well as talk about their implications. How do the API and the databases scale when having multiple databases and what are the Best Practices for avoiding performance issues?

💼 Follow me on LinkedIn and drop me a message if you'd like: https://www.linkedin.com/in/gadirovgs/
💻 Also, let's connect on GitHub: https://github.com/gusgad

RBAC: https://youtu.be/_-tYaw5Z9Gg

Noisy Neighbour pattern: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/antipatterns/noisy-neighbor/noisy-neighbor

And don't forget to subscribe for more videos like this 😊

metadata.title: Advanced Row Level Security (RLS) Policies // Authorization Deep Dive
metadata.author: Supabase
metadata.shortDescription:
Row Level Security (RLS) is a way to implement Authorization in a PostgreSQL database. It automatically denies all select, insert, update and delete requests, unless a policy is written to allow them. In this video, Jon Meyers goes deep with RLS policies, showing how to enforce access rules across related tables.

Full Email Client playlist: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL5S4mPUpp4OumEXnbPS-2rTZnDD58Q12M&feature=shared

Row Level Security (RLS) in Postgres is a powerful feature that allows fine-grained control over which rows in a table can be accessed by different users. By defining policies on tables, you can restrict the visibility and modification of rows based on the attributes of the current user or other conditions. This is particularly useful in multi-tenant applications where you need to ensure that users can only see and manipulate data that belongs to them. RLS policies can be applied to `select`, `insert`, `update`, and `delete` operations, providing a flexible and secure way to enforce data access rules directly at the database level.

01:01 Overview of users schema
02:53 Setting up a relationship across tables in different schemas
05:10 Creating a Trigger Function to insert a new user
09:26 Enabling Row Level Security (RLS)
10:28 Enabling security_invoker to enforce RLS on Views
11:55 Enforcing RLS policies for `select` from related tables
17:03 Writing a `delete` policy across related tables
20:27 Enable `insert` across related tables, using an RLS policy
22:59 Going deeper with RLS

metadata.title: Claude Code + Prisma: Multi-Tenant Postgres API That Can't Leak Data
metadata.author: Alex Rusin
metadata.shortDescription:
Free: 57 auth mistakes that fail a security review 👉 https://blog.alexrusin.com/auth-checklist/?src=yt-multi-tenant-postgres

Postgres Row-Level Security stops multi-tenant data leaks at the database layer. 
Build it in a Node.js + Prisma API with Claude Code — so a query that forgets its 
account filter returns nothing instead of someone else's data.

metadata.title: Implement Authorization using Row Level Security (RLS) with Supabase (Step By Step Guide)
metadata.author: Supabase
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, Jon Meyers explains how Row Level Security (RLS) works, why you should enable it and how to enable RLS / Row Level Policies in Supabase. 

▶ Read more HERE: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth/row-level-security?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_term=jon&utm_content=Ow_Uzedfohk

Jon steps through implementing some common policies using the Supabase Dashboard and demonstrates how rules across multiple tables can work together to restrict access.

PostgreSQL provides a simple syntax for RLS, allowing access rules to be declared in the Database itself. This can make queries more efficient as the client can query the Database directly, without the need for a middleware API.

Additionally, RLS can help to protect the Database against poorly written API code that could potentially leak or compromise sensitive data.

▶ Read more about RLS and Auth HERE: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/auth?utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=social&utm_term=jon&utm_content=Ow_Uzedfohk

Jon from Supabase is back, helping you understand the power and benefits of Row Level Security (RLS) in PostgreSQL, and how easy it actually is to implement in your apps. RLS might sound difficult to implement or something that you can't do yourself, but with Supabase's new AI tools, it's simpler and more accessible than ever - ANYONE can do it.

What you'll learn in the RLS Supabase tutorial video:

✅ Understanding RLS: Discover what RLS is and how it serves as a robust method to implement authorization directly in your PostgreSQL database.

✅Learn the differences between queries NOT using RLS and the benefits of RLS (Row Level Security Policies) and why you REALLY need to start using them!

✅ How to Activate RLS in Supabase SAFELY: Learn how to activate RLS through the Supabase dashboard or by using SQL commands within the Supabase SQL editor, so your tables are securely managed.

✅ Creating and Testing RLS Policies: Step-by-step guidance on writing policies that control who can see, edit, or delete data, demonstrated with practical examples such as managing the visibility of blog posts and comments.

✅ Testing RLS for Specific Users: Find out how to test these policies you’ve set up to see how they behave for different user roles, making sure your application's security is dynamic depending on your policy.

By the end of this tutorial, you'll know how to set up RLS policies for your projects in Supabase, ensuring that your database only reveals what it should to the right users.

We hope this helped you master your database security. Start using RLS with Supabase today!

Chapters: 
0:07 What you’ll learn
0:22 Architecture Without Row Level Security (RLS) - Client, API, PostgreSQL
0:53 Architecture With Row Level Security (RLS) benefits
1:37 How to implement Row Level Security policies in Supabase
2:22 Application using the database
3:20 Use and Enable Row Level Policy
4:52 How to add a new policy
6:31 How to review final RLS policy and show equivalent SQL statement
7:56 Create a new policy so that everyone can see published post
12:56 Create rule/policy for insert
14:30 Create a policy for deleting comments

segments.text: [Music] hey Jon from Supabase here and in this video we're going to learn all about row level
policies now this is a concept that does trip up a lot of people especially if they're new to sql
or even just writing authorization rules at this layer but i promise it's not as scary as it seems
so let's learn how so most people have this mental model of this kind of three-piece architecture
where you have a client an api and a database and the client is only able to directly communicate
with the api and the api is the only thing that's allowed to talk directly to the database so if the
client wants records that are in the database they have to go to the api and they have to say this is
who i am and then the api decides do i trust you or don't i trust you and if they do they're the
only ones that have a special key to the database so they go up to the database get those records um
and then send them back to the client now in the row level security architecture the client can
talk directly to the database and so there's no actual need to have that api in the middle
the client just sends across their authorization token or says who they are to the database
and then the database decides based on those row-level policies should the user have access
to this data or should they not if they should then it can send those results directly to the
client so not only can this make your queries a little bit more efficient because you don't
need to go that extra hop through the api but you also protect yourself from writing some bad logic
in the api that potentially exposes some data from your database by writing the access rules for the
data in the database itself it makes it very hard to accidentally leak out that data because only
the people who should have access to it can have access so let's see how we might implement row
level policies in our own application here i have a blog project that i'm building on Supabase it
has two tables so a post and a comment each post has an id a title the content of the post user id
and so this is the user that authored the blog we then have a created at timestamp and whether or
not the blog is published currently we then have a comment table and again this has an id and content
it has the user that authored the comment a timestamp and then the post that it's associated
with so this just models a fairly common one-to-many relationship where each post has many
comments and every comment belongs to a post so let's have a look at the application that's using
it so here i have a Supabase application i'm going to sign up for a new account as ash pokemon.com
and he can have the super secure password password on the right here we're going to
sign up a second user and so obviously we're going to sign up ash's rival gary at pokemon.com
and he's going to have the same password because i don't think they're very
security conscious over in violet town now ash is going to create a new post so he can give this
post a title and then write about the adventure of his first pokemon and now he's not quite ready
to publish this he thinks that maybe he can add a little bit more to this story so he's just going
to click save and come back to it later and so ash can now see this post he could continue editing it

back to all posts he can see his post listed there which is what we'd expect because even though it

How To Create RLS Policies In Supabase [Step-By-Step 2026]

🌐 Access Supabase Here:
https://supabase.com

🌐 Open Your Dashboard:
https://app.supabase.com

📚 View Docs:
https://supabase.com/docs

In this step-by-step 2026 tutorial, you’ll learn how to create Row Level Security (RLS) policies in Supabase to protect your database and control exactly who can read or modify data. RLS is essential for modern SaaS apps because it enforces permissions directly at the database level. Instead of trusting frontend checks, your backend automatically secures every query.

🔹 What You’ll Learn:
-How To Enable Row Level Security On Tables Inside Supabase
-How To Create SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, And DELETE Policies Safely
-How To Write SQL Conditions That Restrict Access Per User
-How To Use Auth UID Matching For User-Specific Data Isolation
-How To Test Policies Without Breaking Existing Queries
-How To Combine Multiple Policies For Flexible Permissions
-How To Prevent Public Access To Sensitive Records
-How Production Apps Secure Data With Database-Level Rules

💡 Pro Tip: Start with “deny all” policies, then gradually allow specific access. This security-first approach prevents accidental exposure and keeps your database locked down by default.

By the end of this video, you’ll confidently create RLS policies that keep your Supabase backend secure, private, and production-ready.

#Supabase #RLS #DatabaseSecurity #BackendDev #PostgreSQL #Auth #WebDevelopment #SaaS #DevTools #CloudBackend

segments.text: In today's video, I'm going to teach you
how to create RLS policies in Superbase
step-by-step 20-26. Rowle security or
RLS lets you control exactly which rows
a user can read or modify based on who
they are. It's one of the most important
parts of securing your database. And in
Superbase, it's built right into the
dashboard. So, you don't need to wire up
extra middleware to keep data safe.
First, open your browser and go to
superbase.com.
From there, sign into your account using
your usual method. This can be as quick
as using a single sign on provider or
your email and password. Once you're in,
you'll land on the Superbase homepage.
On the homepage, select the organization
that contains the project you want to
work on. Organizations help you keep
projects grouped and permissions tidy.
Pick the one where you'll be adding RLS
so that your changes apply to the right
place. Next, choose your existing
project. If you're starting fresh, you
can create a new project instead. But
I'll proceed with an existing one to
keep things moving. Remember, Subbase
autogenerates a REST API and provides
client libraries like the JavaScript
SDK. So any policy you create here will
immediately govern how your CRUD
operations behave from your app. Inside
the project dashboard, look to the left
sidebar. Click authentication. This is
where Superbase centralizes identity
sessions and related security settings
that policies rely on. Within
authentication, locate configuration.
This houses the settings and sections
you need to define consistent access
rules. Now, click policies. This view is
designed to make policy creation
straightforward while keeping it
powerful. You'll see relevant resources
including tables for which you can set
access rules. You should now see your
listed tables. Choose the table you want
to protect. Then select create policy.
Superbase offers helpful templates on
the left to accelerate common patterns
like letting signed in users access only
their own rows. Pick a template that
matches your intent or start from
scratch if you prefer full control. Give
the policy a clear name and description
so future you and your teammates know
exactly what it does. Choose the
operations the policy applies to, such
as read, insert, update, or delete. Then
define the condition that should pass
for access to be granted. For example,
many apps compare a user identifier in
the row to the current authenticated
user. When you're done, make sure to
save the policy. That's it. You've
navigated to policies, created an RLS
policy, and set the rules your app will
now enforce automatically. Repeat the
process for other tables and actions.
And always test with your app's
authenticated calls to confirm the
behavior matches your expectations.

In this 2026 RLS guide, you’ll learn how to enable Row Level Security in Supabase to protect your database at the deepest level. RLS ensures users only access their own data, preventing leaks and unauthorized reads. It’s one of the most important security features for SaaS and multi-user apps.

In today’s video, we cover supabase policy, create policy supabase, rls in supabase, row level security, supabase tutorial, database security, api policies, supabase setup, data protection, backend development, sql policies, application security, web development tips, supabase features, security best practices, programming tutorials, database management, supabase guide, learn supabase

segments.text: In today's video, I'm going to teach you
how to create policies in Superbase via
dashboard. By the end, you'll know
exactly where to go in the dashboard,
how to enable rowle security, and how to
define a clear policy that controls who
can read or write data in a table. Start
by opening your Superbase project. Log
in. Choose the project you want to work
on and head to the area where you manage
your database. On the left sidebar,
click database, then tables. This takes
you to the table editor which lists all
your tables and gives you a quick way to
manage their structure and security.
Select the table you want to protect
with rowle security.
Inside the table view, switch to the
security or policies tab. Here you can
toggle rowle security on. RLS is a
Postgress feature that lets you filter
data on a per row basis based on who's
making the request. When RLS is enabled,
no one can access table data unless a
policy explicitly allows it. That's by
design and it keeps your data safe. Also
note that if you created the table using
the dashboard's table editor, RLS may
already be enabled by default. Always
double check the toggle so you know the
current state. Next, create a new
policy. In the security or policies tab,
click new policy. The dashboard will
guide you through the policy definition.
Give your policy a clear, descriptive
name so it's obvious what it does later.
Choose the action the policy applies to.
Select for reads, insert for new
records, update for changes, or delete
for removals.
Then select the roles the policy should
cover, such as authenticated users, or
anonymous visitors, depending on your
application's access model. You'll see
two important expressions. The using
expression filters which rows are
accessible for select and also controls
which rows a user can target with update
or delete. The width check expression
applies to insert and update, ensuring
any new or changed rows meet your
conditions before they're accepted. For
example, a common pattern is to allow a
user to see and modify only rows where a
user ID column matches their O user ID.
In that case, you'd mirror that
condition in both using and with check
to enforce the same rule for reading and
writing.
Review your settings, save the policy,
and you're done. Remember that multiple
policies are additive, so a user is
allowed if any matching policy permits
the action. Keeping names clear and
conditions precise will help you
maintain a secure, predictable setup as
your app grows.
