metadata.title: AI Model Routing Explained: Cut LLM Costs With LiteLLM
metadata.author: Hunter Sneed
metadata.shortDescription:
Your AI bill is not going to fix itself. If every request goes to the newest frontier model, you’re not being “safe” - you’re probably wasting a ton of money.

In this video, I break down tokenomics, model routing, LiteLLM, fallback providers, and how to build an AI stack that sends the right request to the right model. The goal is simple: keep the quality, own the bill, and stop treating every LLM call like it deserves the most expensive model available.

I’ll show you how a model router classifies requests, routes simple work to cheaper models, escalates harder work to stronger models, verifies outputs with evals, and gives you observability into token spend by workload, user, tenant, department, or app.

Model Router Demo Repo ⬇️
Download: https://gettingautomated.com/guides/own-the-bill-ai-model-router

🔥 What You'll Learn
• Why tokenomics is becoming one of the biggest AI problems for businesses
• Why defaulting everything to the best model is expensive and usually unnecessary
• How model routers classify requests by complexity, risk, accuracy needs, and cost
• When cheaper models are “good enough” and when frontier models are actually worth it
• How LiteLLM helps with routing, retries, fallbacks, usage logs, budgets, and observability
• Why fallback models matter when providers go down, models get pulled, or APIs degrade
• How evals keep quality under control when you start routing across multiple models
• Where routers fit compared to native SDKs, LangChain, Vercel AI, OpenRouter, Bedrock, Vertex, and Azure Foundry

🧠 The Model Router Pattern
• Request Classifier - looks at the incoming task and estimates difficulty
• Routing Policy - decides whether cost, speed, quality, or reliability matters most
• Model Tiers - cheap, standard, and frontier models for different task types
• Verifier / Eval - checks whether the output actually met the goal
• Escalation - retries with a stronger model when confidence or quality is too low
• Fallback Providers - keeps your AI features alive when one provider has an outage
• Telemetry - tracks logs, token spend, caching, latency, and cost by workload

💻 Demo / Process Overview
• Run a batch of real example requests through a model router
• Watch the classifier pick the starting model for each task
• Compare routed cost against an “all premium model” baseline
• See why some requests can safely go to cheaper models while others need escalation
• Use LiteLLM logs to inspect requests, model choices, spend, and usage patterns
• Tag requests by user, tenant, workload, or department for better cost visibility
• Add fallback behavior so your app doesn’t break when one model or provider goes down

⚠️ What to Watch Out For
• Routers are not magic - they need good policies and evals
• Cheap models can save money, but only if the output is still good enough
• Logging every prompt and response can create security and privacy problems
• A router is great for API-driven workloads, but it does not replace Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, or the native app experience
• Cost savings depend on your workload mix - some teams may save 20%, others may save 50–70%+
• The real goal is not “use the cheapest model” - it’s “use the right model for the job”

metadata.title: LiteLLM AI Gateway: Routing, API Keys, Budgets, and Guardrails for Local and Cloud Models
metadata.author: Paul Zuradzki
metadata.shortDescription:
I demo using LiteLLM as a provider-agnostic Python SDK and self-hosted AI gateway for routing, keying, and budgeting between local and cloud models. Worthy feature mentions not covered in the video: guardrails, policies, logging.

0:00 Intro: the two parts of LiteLLM
0:13 Python SDK: one completion function for any OpenAI-compatible provider
0:54 AI gateway: self-hosted, in front of local and cloud models
1:41 80/20 goal: 80% local, 20% cloud for cost and privacy
2:02 Wiring up a coding agent: pi's models.json pointed at one LiteLLM provider
3:39 Shared API keys without exposing your local network
4:03 Key management: model scoping, budgets, and simulated pricing for local models
5:01 Estimating avoided inference cost on your own hardware
5:27 Guardrails and policies: content filtering and PII protection
6:06 Sample structure for two GPUs: llama.cpp + llama-swap behind LiteLLM
7:42 Ollama vs. llama.cpp
8:57 Wrap-up

metadata.title: How We Built a $1.5M ARR SaaS With 3 People and $0 in Ad Spend
metadata.author: MicroConf
metadata.shortDescription:
Marie Martens, co-founder of Tally, shares how she and her partner Filip Minev bootstrapped a freemium form builder from zero to $1.5M ARR with a team of just three people and no paid advertising. 

In this MicroConf Europe 2024 talk, Marie walks through the full journey: from a failed travel tech startup and a pandemic pivot, to building a product-led growth engine powered by a generous free plan, community-driven word of mouth, and radically simple product design.

She covers how they found their first users through cold outreach on Product Hunt, launched successfully after six months of preparation, and grew through a flywheel where free forms with Tally branding drive organic discovery. 

Marie also shares the hard lessons — handling 400,000 users with no support team, learning to say no, navigating abuse and phishing on their platform, shifting from remote digital nomad life to a physical office, and evolving from indie hackers into company builders.

Key topics in this talk:
— Freemium pricing strategy for bootstrapped SaaS
— Product-led growth without paid marketing
— Cold outreach tactics for early user acquisition

metadata.title: LLM Model Routing: Cut AI API Costs by 80 Percent
metadata.author: Webronaq
metadata.shortDescription:
LLM model routing cost optimization: stop paying frontier prices for every request and cut your AI API bill by 40 to 80 percent without capping access or slowing your team down.

In June 2026, Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong revealed that his company cut its internal AI spend nearly in half while token usage kept growing, by deploying an LLM gateway that routes each request to the cheapest capable model and pushed its cache hit rate from 5 percent to 60 percent. That real-world result lines up with peer-reviewed research: the RouteLLM paper, published at ICLR 2025 by LMSYS, demonstrated 85 percent cost savings while retaining 95 percent of frontier-model quality. This video breaks down exactly how LLM routing works, the three routing strategies every team should know, and which tools to use to build it yourself today.

In this video:
- What an LLM router (AI gateway) is and how it intercepts and routes every model request
- The Coinbase LLM gateway playbook: smarter defaults, task-based routing, and aggressive caching
- Three routing strategies compared: rule-based routing, complexity classifier, and cascade routing
- LiteLLM vs Portkey vs OpenRouter: which LLM gateway tool fits your stack in 2026
- A practical five-step checklist to implement LLM cost optimization in your own application

Subscribe to Webronaq for clear, practical lessons on computer science, AI, and software engineering:
https://www.youtube.com/@Webronaq

#LLMmodelrouting #AIcostoptimization #LLMgateway #AIProgramming #Webronaq

segments.text: Hello friends, and welcome. Here is a number that should get your attention. Enterprise spending on
generative AI jumped from 11.5 billion dollars in 2024 to 37 billion dollars in 2025. That is more
than triple in a single year, according to Menlo Ventures. And token usage is still climbing fast.
So teams that wired everything to one expensive frontier model are watching their bills compound
every month. The normal fix companies reach for is to cap access, set alerts, and slow engineers
down. But in late June 2026, Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong posted a very different answer. He said
Coinbase had cut its AI spend nearly in half while token usage kept growing exponentially. The lever
he used was not a spending cap. It was an LLM router. Let me show you exactly what that is.
So what exactly is an LLM router? Think of it as a traffic controller that sits between
your application and the model providers. Your app sends every request to the router first.
The router reads the request, decides which model is the cheapest one capable of handling it,
and forwards it there. A simple autocomplete or a quick summary goes to a small, cheap model. A
complex multi-step reasoning task gets sent to a powerful frontier model. The key insight is that
most requests do not need the most expensive model. If you are paying frontier prices for
all of them, you are just leaving money on the table. The router also handles caching,
so if the same question comes in again, it returns the stored answer and skips the
model call entirely. One gateway, one endpoint, intelligent decisions on every single request.
Now let us see exactly how Coinbase did it. Armstrong outlined three levers,
all working inside an LLM gateway. Lever one: smarter defaults. The gateway routes
engineers to open-weight models, specifically GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.7, as the starting point.
These are capable models that cost a fraction of a frontier subscription. Engineers can still choose
a stronger model when the task calls for it, but the default is the cheaper option. Lever two:
task-based routing. The gateway looks at each request and matches it to the cheapest
model that can actually handle it. Routine tasks stay on the small models. Only genuinely complex
work escalates to a frontier model. Lever three: caching. Coinbase pushed its cache hit rate from
5 percent to 60 percent. That means 60 percent of requests never even reached a model at all.
The result: token usage grew, the bill shrank, and 91 percent of engineers never hit a usage cap. And
coming up, we will break down the three routing strategies you can use to build this yourself.
Alright, so Coinbase used all three of the main routing strategies at once. Let's break them down
so you know which one fits which situation. The first is rule-based routing. The router
checks each request against a set of keywords or patterns. If the message matches a simple pattern,
it goes straight to the cheap model. This adds under 1 millisecond of overhead,
so it is essentially free. Great when your request types are predictable. The second
is a complexity classifier. A small machine learning model reads the request and scores
how hard it is. Simple requests go to the small model, complex ones escalate to the
frontier. The catch is a 50 to 100 millisecond overhead per request. The third is cascade
routing. The cheap model answers first. If its output passes a quality check, you are done.
If not, the request escalates automatically to the frontier model. Research on cascade
routing has demonstrated cost reductions of up to 85 percent. More intelligence,
but two sequential calls on the hard cases. Coming up, we will match each strategy to the right tool.
Now let us match a strategy to a real tool. There are three strong options in 2026. First, LiteLLM.
It is an MIT-licensed, self-hosted proxy that unifies more than 100 providers behind a single
endpoint. You get cost-based routing, caching with Redis, and spend tracking. Pick this when you want
full control over your own infrastructure. Second, Portkey. In March 2026, Portkey released Gateway
2.0 as fully open source under Apache 2.0, opening its entire production feature set to self-hosters.
That includes semantic caching, guardrails for PII redaction, and support for more than 1,600
models. It is the strongest pick for teams in regulated industries. Third, OpenRouter. This
is the managed option. No servers to run. You get instant access to more than 300 models and pay per
token with no infrastructure overhead. Perfect for teams that want to start routing today without any
ops burden. Each tool supports cascade and fallback patterns, so the strategy from the
last slide works with all three. Next, a practical checklist to get this running in your own stack.
Here is the practical starting checklist. Step one: instrument before you optimize. You need to
see which endpoints and request types are burning the most tokens. You cannot route what you cannot
measure. Step two: route the easy stuff first. Pick your highest-volume, simplest task, something
like short summaries or autocomplete, and send it to a capable open-weight model. That single change
often covers most of your bill. Step three: enable prompt caching at the gateway. Coinbase took its
cache hit rate from 5 percent to 60 percent. Even a 30 percent hit rate meaningfully cuts
costs. Step four: add a quality fallback chain. Define a simple check on the small model's output.
If it fails, escalate to the frontier. You keep quality high without paying frontier prices for
everything. Step five: review your model selection quarterly. Pricing in this space shifts fast,
and new capable models arrive constantly. A routing layer that works today can work even
harder in three months with a quick refresh. That is the whole playbook. Start simple,
measure everything, and layer in complexity as the savings justify it. Thanks for watching.

metadata.title: I Built an Auto Router for Local LLMs with LiteLLM + Pi Coding Agent
metadata.author: Execute Automation
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, I build an Auto Router for multiple local LLMs using LiteLLM, Pi Coding Agent, Ollama, and oMLX. Instead of sending every request to the biggest model, the router classifies the task and decides whether it should go to a smaller, faster model or a larger, more capable one.

The setup uses models like Qwen3.5 4B, Gemma 4, and Qwen3.8 27B, running across Ollama and oMLX. I also show the difference between LiteLLM’s heuristic classifier and an LLM-powered classifier, and how this kind of routing can reduce unnecessary memory pressure and improve overall local AI throughput on Apple Silicon.

metadata.shortDescription:
Which micro SaaS examples are actually real in 2026? These eight are live today, make $1M to $8M a year, and every figure comes from the founder or a public source. Three products that appear on almost every other list were cut for raising venture capital.

See what 8,000 SaaS startups actually earn: https://bigideasdb.com

A micro SaaS is a software product that solves one narrow problem for one audience, run by one to about ten people and funded by its own revenue rather than investors. Across the tracked set, the average micro SaaS makes $4,298 a month, the median $145, and 6.1% clear $10,000 a month.

THE 8 MICRO SAAS EXAMPLES, RANKED BY REVENUE

#8 Bannerbear, image generation API, about $1M a year. Jon Yongfook, solo, after twelve failed products.
#7 Testimonial.to, video testimonial collection, over $1M a year. Damon Chen, solo.
#6 Typefully, thread writing and scheduling for X, around $113K a month.
#5 Photo AI, AI headshots and photos, around $130K a month. Pieter Levels, zero employees.
#4 Tally, form builder with unlimited free forms, around $150K a month.
#3 Rezi, AI resume builder, around $200K a month.
#2 Plausible, privacy focused web analytics, around $3.5M a year. Uku Täht and Marko Saric, about ten people, open source.
#1 Submagic, automatic captions for short form video, $8M a year. David Zitoun, 13 people, no investors.

Motion, Copy.ai and Carrd were cut. Motion raised $60M at a $550M valuation, Copy.ai raised about $16.9M and was acquired by Fullcast, and Carrd took $2M from Shrug Capital and Flybridge. Real businesses, not micro SaaS.

WHAT THE EIGHT HAVE IN COMMON

One sharp feature aimed at a workflow people repeat every day.
A free layer that spreads, and a paid layer a business cannot ship without.
Built on revenue by one to thirteen people, with pricing that follows the stakes of the problem.

The method behind the list: check what products in a niche already earn before you build anything. BigIdeasDB runs that check across 8,000+ SaaS startups, with category margins, growth data and a free idea evaluator.

Whimo, their self-driving car company,

AI systems can model complex

simultaneously. That means you could

new agents from the Oz web app or CLI,
or set them up on schedules and event
triggers. But once they're live, you can
watch them work and steer things as
needed. Try running your own agent today
at the link below and use the code
fireship for a special discount. This
has been the code report. Thanks for
watching and I will see you in the next
one.

metadata.title: The Micro-SaaS Receipts: The 'Passive MRR' Dream vs The Churn Math
metadata.author: Hustle Audit
metadata.shortDescription: Early this morning we're investigating the 'build a micro-SaaS for passive monthly recurring revenue' dream, and audits it against the churn math, the failure data, and the honest odds. The pitch is seductive: write the code once, charge a small monthly fee, and watch recurring revenue compound while you sleep. The reality most builders hit is 'build it and they won't come', a polished launch that lands in silence, because the hard part was never the code; it was getting a stranger to find, trust, and pay. We walk the MRR-and-churn economics: why every subscription business hits a ceiling equal to new MRR divided by monthly churn (add $1,000/mo in new MRR at 5% churn and revenue flatlines near $20,000 MRR; at 7% churn it caps closer to $14,300), and why churn scales with your size so 'passive' income is really a bucket with a hole you refill forever. We cite the measured benchmarks: Baremetrics open-benchmark data puts under-$10 ARPU products near 6.2% monthly user churn and consumer apps in the 6.5–8% range, with under 5% monthly considered solid, meaning a base can lose more than half its revenue in a year with no new sales. We cover why customer acquisition cost and distribution, not code, are the real bottleneck (in one large study of failed founders, marketing problems, chiefly no product-market fit, drove over half of failures), the survivorship bias baked into 'indie hacker' success stories, and the honest odds: roughly nine in ten startups fail, most micro-SaaS never clears a few hundred dollars a month, a thin slice reach what Paul Graham called 'ramen profitable' (just enough to cover the founder's living costs), and a vanishingly small number become the life-changing wins that fill the highlight reels. Distinct from our indie-app-revenue receipts, this one focuses on the SaaS subscription/MRR model specifically.

segments.text: The pitch is one of the most seductive
in all of online business.
You are a developer or you are willing
to learn. You build a small piece of
software that solves one narrow boring
problem.
People pay you a modest fee every single
month to keep using it. You do the work
once and the money arrives while you
sleep month after month, a quiet river
of recurring revenue that grows on its
own. They call it micro software as a
service and the dream bolted to it is
passive monthly recurring revenue. It is
real for a few.
For most, the story ends very
differently. So we pulled the churn
math, the failure data, and the honest
odds, and audited the dream against the
numbers. Start with why the dream is so
magnetic because the logic underneath it
genuinely holds together right up until
the moment it does not. A traditional
business trades your hours for money.
Software breaks that link. You write the
code once and in theory the same code
serves one customer or 10,000 at almost
no extra cost.
Stack a subscription on top and each
customer does not pay you once but keeps
paying month after month.
In the language of the trade, you are
building monthly recurring revenue and
recurring revenue compounds.
Land a handful of paying users this
month, keep them, add a handful more
next month, and the line marches upward
on its own.
On a whiteboard, it is the closest thing
to a money printer that ordinary people
can legally build.
The only question an audit has to ask is
what happens when the whiteboard meets
the market. Here is what usually happens
when it does. A founder spends weeks,
sometimes months, lovingly building the
product. They obsess over the features,
the design, the landing page. Finally,
they launch.
They post it on a forum, share it with a
few friends, hit publish, and then they
sit back and wait for the river of
recurring revenue to start flowing.
And what comes back is silence, a
trickle of curious visitors, a handful
of free signups,
and almost no one willing to actually
pay.
Builders have a name for this outcome.
Build and they will not come.
The hardest part of the whole endeavor
turns out not to be writing the software
at all.
It is getting a single stranger to find
it, trust it, and hand over a card.
The code was the easy part.
The market was the wall. Now walk the
numbers the dream conveniently skips.
Suppose you are good. Suppose every
month you manage to add $1,000 in new
recurring revenue, a genuinely strong
result for a solo founder. It sounds
like you would cross $10,000 a month
inside of a year, but subscriptions
leak. Every month some customers cancel,
and that lost revenue has a name, churn.
And here is the trap almost no one sees
coming. Your revenue does not climb
forever. It climbs only until the money
you lose to churn each month equals the
money you add. At that point the growth
flatlines, no matter how hard you push,
and the ceiling is brutally simple to
calculate. Take the new revenue you add
each month and divide it by your monthly
churn rate.
That one division is the invisible wall
every subscription business eventually
slams into. Sit with what that ceiling
really means because it is the single
most important idea in the whole
business.
Every subscription company is running up
a downward escalator.
Churn is the escalator carrying
customers away, and your marketing is
your effort to climb faster than it
descends.
Early on, with a tiny customer base, the
losses are small and the growth feels
effortless, but churn is a percentage,
so the bigger you get, the more
customers you bleed every month in raw
numbers, and the harder you have to run
just to hold your ground.
Growth does not slow because you got
lazy.
It slows because the leak scales with
your success.
A business quietly losing a slice of its
customers every month is not passive at
all. It is a bucket with a hole, and you
are the one condemned to keep refilling
it forever, and these are not scary
hypotheticals. They are the measured
averages.
Open benchmark data on real subscription
companies shows that the cheaper your
price, the faster customers leave.
Products charging under $10 a month see
roughly six of every 100 customers
cancel every single month. Consumer
facing apps, which is classic micro
software territory, churn even harder,
often in the range of 1 to 8% monthly.
Industry guides call anything under 5% a
month solid ground.
Now, do the arithmetic on 6% monthly
churn, and you find that with no new
sales at all, a subscription base loses
more than half its revenue in under a
year. That is the current your little
money printer is swimming against from
the very first day it goes live. So, if
the code is easy and the churn is
relentless, what actually decides
whether a micro software business lives
or dies?
The answer is the least glamorous word
in all of technology.
Distribution.
Getting in front of strangers, earning
their trust, and convincing them to pay

videos.full_text: The pitch is one of the most seductive in all of online business. You are a developer or you are willing to learn. You build a small piece of software that solves one narrow boring problem. People pay you a modest fee every single month to keep using it. You do the work once and the money arrives while you sleep month after month, a quiet river of recurring revenue that grows on its own. They call it micro software as a service and the dream bolted to it is passive monthly recurring revenue. It is real for a few. For most, the story ends very differently. So we pulled the churn math, the failure data, and the honest odds, and audited the dream against the numbers. Start with why the dream is so magnetic because the logic underneath it genuinely holds together right up until the moment it does not. A traditional business trades your hours for money. Software breaks that link. You write the code once and in theory the same code serves one customer or 10,000 at almost no extra cost. Stack a subscription on top and each customer does not pay you once but keeps paying month after month. In the language of the trade, you are building monthly recurring revenue and recurring revenue compounds. Land a handful of paying users this month, keep them, add a handful more next month, and the line marches upward on its own. On a whiteboard, it is the closest thing to a money printer that ordinary people can legally build. The only question an audit has to ask is what happens when the whiteboard meets the market. Here is what usually happens when it does. A founder spends weeks, sometimes months, lovingly building the product. They obsess over the features, the design, the landing page. Finally, they launch. They post it on a forum, share it with a few friends, hit publish, and then they sit back and wait for the river of recurring revenue to start flowing. And what comes back is silence, a trickle of curious visitors, a handful of free signups, and almost no one willing to actually pay. Builders have a name for this outcome. Build and they will not come. The hardest part of the whole endeavor turns out not to be writing the software at all. It is getting a single stranger to find it, trust it, and hand over a card. The code was the easy part. The market was the wall. Now walk the numbers the dream conveniently skips. Suppose you are good. Suppose every month you manage to add $1,000 in new recurring revenue, a genuinely strong result for a solo founder. It sounds like you would cross $10,000 a month inside of a year, but subscriptions leak. Every month some customers cancel, and that lost revenue has a name, churn. And here is the trap almost no one sees coming. Your revenue does not climb forever. It climbs only until the money you lose to churn each month equals the money you add. At that point the growth flatlines, no matter how hard you push, and the ceiling is brutally simple to calculate. Take the new revenue you add each month and divide it by your monthly churn rate. That one division is the invisible wall every subscription business eventually slams into. Sit with what that ceiling really means because it is the single most important idea in the whole business. Every subscription company is running up a downward escalator. Churn is the escalator carrying customers away, and your marketing is your effort to climb faster than it descends. Early on, with a tiny customer base, the losses are small and the growth feels effortless, but churn is a percentage, so the bigger you get, the more customers you bleed every month in raw numbers, and the harder you have to run just to hold your ground. Growth does not slow because you got lazy. It slows because the leak scales with your success. A business quietly losing a slice of its customers every month is not passive at all. It is a bucket with a hole, and you are the one condemned to keep refilling it forever, and these are not scary hypotheticals. They are the measured averages. Open benchmark data on real subscription companies shows that the cheaper your price, the faster customers leave. Products charging under $10 a month see roughly six of every 100 customers cancel every single month. Consumer facing apps, which is classic micro software territory, churn even harder, often in the range of 1 to 8% monthly. Industry guides call anything under 5% a month solid ground. Now, do the arithmetic on 6% monthly churn, and you find that with no new sales at all, a subscription base loses more than half its revenue in under a year. That is the current your little money printer is swimming against from the very first day it goes live. So, if the code is easy and the churn is relentless, what actually decides whether a micro software business lives or dies? The answer is the least glamorous word in all of technology. Distribution. Getting in front of strangers, earning their trust, and convincing them to pay over and over, cheaply enough that you still profit. Every customer costs something to acquire in advertising, in content, in time. That is your acquisition cost, and for a low price subscription that a customer might keep for only a few months, the math is savage. And when the founders of failed startups are asked what actually killed them, the largest single cause by a wide margin is not bad code, and it is not thin funding. In one large study of failed founders, marketing problems, chiefly the failure to find a real market, accounted for more than half of all the deaths. The bottleneck was never the building, it was the selling, which brings us to the odds nobody prints on the core sales page. startups as a class mostly fail. The widely cited figure is that around nine in every 10 of them do not make it. Micro software sits squarely inside that grim distribution. The overwhelming majority of products launched never reach even a few hundred dollars a month in lasting revenue, and they quietly die within a year or two. A thin slice climb to what the investor Paul Graham famously named ramen profitable, making just enough to cover the founders basic living costs, and a vanishingly small number become the life changing successes that fill the highlight reels. The real shape of it is not a ladder that everyone climbs. It is a lottery with a very long tail and a floor that most people quietly land on. And this is where the story you are told bends the truth without ever technically lying. Every screenshot of a soaring revenue chart, every founder crowing about the product they built in a weekend that now prints thousands a month is real. But it is also a survivor handpicked from a graveyard you never get to see. For every indie builder posting their winning dashboard, there are dozens, hundreds who launched the very same kind of product, watched the same silence, and quietly shut it down without ever posting a word. Their flat charts do not trend on social media. Their stories are not sold to you as courses. This is survivorship bias in its purest form. The winners are loud and visible. The failures are silent and invisible. And you are gently invited to mistake the loud, rare exception for the normal expected result. So what is the honest verdict on the software dream? It is not a scam, and that is exactly what makes it dangerous. The model genuinely works. Recurring revenue is genuinely powerful and a real, if small, share of builders do reach that ramen profitable floor and a few climb far beyond it. But the version sold to you of passive money arriving while you sleep because you once wrote some clever code is a fantasy that leaves out the two things that actually decide the outcome. Relentless churn and the brutal, unglamorous grind of distribution. Build a software product if you love solving the problem and you can stomach years of selling it. Just walk in knowing the code was never the hard part. The odds live in a very long tail and the money was never, for one single moment, passive.

metadata.title: How I Scaled a Micro SaaS With SEO to 300€ MRR
metadata.author: Micael Coutinho
metadata.shortDescription:
I scaled my micro SaaS, MockClip, to 300€ MRR using SEO as my main distribution channel. Here’s the exact setup, the weekly routine, the real results, and what I’d do differently if I started over.

SEO is cheaper than social media to start, and the content keeps working for longer. It’s also slow: I waited at least 6 months for meaningful results, and Bing took almost 10 months to start sending traffic. In this video I cover who SEO is not for, the technical setup I used, and the simple weekly indexing routine that made the difference. Then I go through an honest good, bad and ugly review of the numbers: about 1,000 search clicks, and why I’d still do it, but never as my only channel again.

🛠️ TOOLS MENTIONED
Google Lighthouse: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse
Seobility: https://www.seobility.net
Google Search Console: https://search.google.com/search-console
Bing Webmaster Tools: https://www.bing.com/webmasters
IndexNow: https://www.indexnow.org

🎬 MockClip, the fake app video generator from this video: https://mockclip.com

I’m Micael, an engineer building micro SaaS products alongside a full-time job and sharing the real numbers, the mistakes and what actually worked. New video every week.

metadata.title: SaaS Metrics Dashboard in Excel | LayerGryph Tutorial (MRR, Churn, Cohorts, LTV to CAC)
metadata.author: LayerGryph
metadata.shortDescription:
A 3-minute walkthrough of the LayerGryph SaaS Metrics Dashboard for Excel and Google Sheets: set your benchmarks, keep one list of customers, and watch the MRR waterfall, cohorts, churn, unit economics and a one-page board summary build themselves.

Get the template: https://layergryph.etsy.com/listing/4609182200/saas-metrics-dashboard-excel-google
Also on Gumroad: https://gum.co/u/1nmcdjhd

CHAPTERS
0:00 Intro
0:16 Step 1: Start Here & Setup
0:44 Step 2: Customers
0:55 Step 3: MRR Movement
1:15 Step 4: Dashboard
1:31 Cohorts, Churn & Retention
1:50 Unit Economics
2:02 Forecast & Board Summary
2:15 Make it your own with AI
2:52 Wrap-up

WHAT'S INSIDE
• 10 tabs: Start Here, Setup, Dashboard, Customers, MRR Movement, Cohorts, Churn & Retention, Unit Economics, Forecast, Board Summary
• An MRR waterfall that reconciles every month: new, expansion, contraction and churn
• A cohort retention triangle, plus logo churn, GRR and NRR, each with a verdict
• CAC by channel, LTV, LTV to CAC and payback, with every formula explained in plain English
• A twelve-month forecast and a one-page board summary
• Works in Excel 2013+ (Windows or Mac) and Google Sheets — no macros, no add-ins, no account to connect

MAKE IT YOUR OWN
The dashboard is a foundation you can build on. Set your own benchmarks, rename your plans, segments and channels, or pair it with an AI assistant like Copilot in Excel, Gemini in Google Sheets, ChatGPT or Claude to ask questions about your customers and add new features.

This video shows sample data. It is a reporting tool, not financial advice.

#excel #saas #startup

retention is getting better or worse.

Claude.

reason.

AI features depend on your Microsoft or
Google plan.
That's it. Board Ready SaaS metrics from
one simple customer list. It's a
modeling tool, not financial advice.
Find the link in the description, and
thanks for watching.

metadata.title: AI Generated Apps vs SaaS: Which Moats Still Work in 2026
metadata.author: MicroConf
metadata.shortDescription:
AI generated apps are reshaping SaaS, but not all SaaS moats are dead. Here's which defensible moats still work, and which ones AI just demolished.

📈 SUBSCRIBE: https://www.youtube.com/@MicroConf?sub_confirmation=1
🎟️ Join us at the next MicroConf: https://microconf.com/upcoming-events

In this talk from MicroConf US 2026: Portland, DNSimple founder Anthony Eden breaks down what the rise of generative AI and one-user vibe-coded apps actually means for SaaS founders. Drawing on 16 years of building DNSimple against competitors ranging from Google, Microsoft, and Amazon down to scrappy new entrants, Anthony separates the SaaS moats that are evaporating from the ones that still defend a business in 2026 and beyond.

You'll learn:
- Why features, integrations, and high switching costs no longer count as defensible moats
- How collaboration and network effects remain a structural advantage AI can't replicate
- Why regulated environments (medical, safety, compliance) are getting harder, not easier, for generative apps to enter
- How operational excellence becomes more valuable as AI generates more low-quality code
- Why capex-heavy infrastructure (DNS, payments, IP management) is still a moat
- What the bifurcation of SaaS looks like — and how to position your business on the right side of it

Anthony Eden is the founder and CEO of DNSimple, which he has run for 16 years competing against hyperscalers and indie startups alike. He is also actively building a second business using generative AI tools, giving him a perspective from both sides of the shift.

This talk was recorded live at MicroConf US 2026: Portland.

metadata.title: How to Get Your SaaS Recommended by ChatGPT (What Actually Works)
metadata.author: Paul Ogonowski
metadata.shortDescription:
Tally, the form builder, got 44% of a record week's 40,000 signups from AI assistants. 44%! Here's how to find your own number, get recommended by ChatGPT more often and track it every week.

Three steps: Ask, Fix, Track. The five things that get you cited (and the five I'd skip) are in the write-up, with every source linked.

🛠 Free skill that tracks your prompts every week (ChatGPT, Gemini, Google's AI Overviews): https://owneropsguide.substack.com/p/ai-shortlist-check-skill
📖 The full write-up with sources: https://owneropsguide.substack.com/p/saas-cited-by-ai-search
📬 The Anti-Grind SaaS Manual, one playbook every two weeks for B2B SaaS founders who can't be the whole GTM anymore: https://owneropsguide.substack.com/subscribe
💻 Source code of the skill: https://github.com/pogonow/operator-toolkit

Homework: run five of your buyer prompts in ChatGPT today and tell me in the comments how many of them name you. I'll go first.

Chapters 
0:00 Tally got 44% of signups from AI
0:34 Why your analytics can't see it
1:00 Step 1: Ask every signup where they came from
3:14 1. "Best for" lists and honest vs pages
4:54 2. Fix your G2 profile
6:08 3. Use-case pages and how-to videos
7:07 4. Pricing bots can read
8:06 5. Original data
8:36 Getting on other people's lists
9:33 What I'd skip (llms.txt, schema and more)
10:22 Step 3: Track 15 to 25 buyer prompts
11:35 The free skill and your homework

Sources: Marie Martens (Tally), Pew Research, Ahrefs, Siege Media, G2's 2026 buyer survey, Growth Unhinged, SparkToro and Gumshoe, Kyle Poyar and Maja Voje's 2026 State of B2B GTM. All linked in the write-up.

About me: I've run growth and GTM in B2B since 2008, 3x founder with 2 exits. I write The Anti-Grind SaaS Manual for founders handing off GTM without breaking it. LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/pawelogonowski/

metadata.title: Vertical AI shows potential to dwarf legacy SaaS | State of the Cloud 2024
metadata.author: Bessemer Venture Partners
metadata.shortDescription:
Caty Rea, Kent Bennett, and Brian Feinstein of Bessemer Venture Partners discuss how Vertical AI is a 10x bigger opportunity than legacy vertical SaaS. Three new business models are transforming how businesses will operate in every industry.  

State of the Cloud 2024 report is now out — https://www.bvp.com/atlas/state-of-the-cloud-2024

Top takeaways: 
— Vertical AI is expected to have a market capitalization at least 10 times the size of legacy Vertical SaaS by targeting high-cost repetitive language-based tasks across various industries, potentially transforming sectors like business and professional services, which are significant portions of the economy.
— Three new business models of Vertical AI include: Copilots, Agents, and AI-enabled Services
— The first Vertical AI IPO is expected within the next three years.
— At least five Vertical AI companies are predicted to reach $100M+ ARR (Centaurs) within the next two to three years.

metadata.title: Metronome + Stripe: Usage-Based Billing in PeakCommerce
metadata.author: PeakCommerce
metadata.shortDescription:
The Metronome integration in PeakCommerce brings usage-based and consumption billing — metered products, prepaid credits, tiered rates — into the same catalog and journeys you use for subscriptions, with invoices collected through a linked Stripe integration. Metronome finalizes the invoices; Stripe holds the payment method and collects automatically. In this guide you'll connect Metronome with a securely stored API token, then see how journeys do the talking: a step's commerce action routed through the Metronome integration — choose the operation, from creating the subscription to applying a retention offer, map the journey's own data into the call, and every customer who reaches that step fires it automatically.

Integrations live under Settings → Integrations; commerce actions live on journey steps in the builder.

Learn more: https://docs.peakcommerce.com

metadata.title: How to Add Credit-Based Billing to Your AI SaaS (Step-by-Step)
metadata.author: Dodo Payments
metadata.shortDescription:
Building credit-based billing or token systems for an AI SaaS is painful.
You end up writing ledger logic, handling credit rollovers, managing overages, setting balance alerts, and wiring everything into subscriptions.

That’s weeks of work just for billing infrastructure.

In this video, we show how to integrate Dodo Payments Credit-Based Billing into an AI chatbot platform end-to-end.

The demo app supports multiple AI models like DeepSeek, Qwen, GPT and more, and we’ll add a credit system so users are billed based on usage.

You'll see how to:

• Set up Dodo Payments dashboard
• Create meters for AI token usage
• Configure credit entitlements
• Create subscription products
• Implement checkout flow
• Track usage events for token consumption
• Handle low balance alerts with webhooks
• Fetch real-time credit balances

By the end of the video, you'll have a fully working credit-based billing system for your AI app.

Credit Based Billing: https://docs.dodopayments.com/features/credit-based-billing

Github: https://github.com/dodopayments/chat-ai

metadata.title: How to Add Stripe Subscriptions to Your SvelteKit App
metadata.author: The Bridge Dev
metadata.shortDescription:
👉 Try The Bridge for free: https://thebridge.dev/yt/code20

Add subscriptions and payments to your SvelteKit app with Stripe: a free and a pro plan, Stripe checkout, features locked by plan and usage-based pricing, set up by your AI coding agent (Claude Code) with The Bridge.

In this SvelteKit billing tutorial you'll see how to:
• Connect your app to The Bridge through the MCP server in Claude Code
• Create a Free and a Pro plan ($9/month) and add Stripe checkout with one prompt
• Lock premium features to the Pro plan and unlock them when a user upgrades
• Test a real payment flow with a Stripe test card
• See exactly what changed in your code, and why there's no billing logic in it (plans and features live in The Bridge, your code just checks a flag)
• Add usage limits and metered billing: 1 QR code a month on Free, 3 on Pro, then $1 for each extra one, and track usage in the dashboard
• Change prices, features and limits later without touching your code

We use QR Studio, a simple QR code generator built with SvelteKit, as the example app. The same steps work for any SvelteKit or Svelte project.

7:18 Adding a limit and charging for extra use
10:01 Wrap-up

The Bridge gives your app authentication, feature flags, billing and teams in one place, so you can stop wiring up separate services and get back to building your product.

This discussion explores the rise of the #microsaas model, demonstrating how a #solopreneur can build a successful #saas product like Sync to Sheets, generating significant #recurringrevenue. We highlight how a #onepersonbusiness can thrive with minimal resources, offering a playbook for aspiring entrepreneurs.

A freelance developer built Sync to Sheets in two weeks. It syncs Notion to Google Sheets. It now makes $9,000/month with 400+ paying customers. Meanwhile, enterprise SaaS companies are watching hundreds of billions evaporate. Something fundamental has changed. In this episode, I break down the data, share 3 real micro-SaaS case studies, and give you the 5-step playbook for building your own.

Key takeaways:
• Micro-SaaS market: $16B (2024) -- $60B by 2030 at ~30% CAGR
• 39% of independent SaaS founders are solo operators
• Median profitable micro-SaaS: ~$4,200/month MRR. Top 1%: $50K+/month.
• 3 advantages: AI collapsed build costs, niche beats horizontal, distribution is the moat
• Sync to Sheets: $9K/mo, 400+ customers, built in 2 weeks, monthly costs under $90
• Chatbase: $64K/mo in 6 months, no paid ads to $50K MRR, rode the ChatGPT wave
• Receipt AI: dead simple (photo -- accounting), LLM-powered, solves real annoyance
• 5-step playbook: find pain, solve one thing, build in weeks, price for value, pick one channel
• AI startups: up to 30x revenue valuations. $100K/yr micro-SaaS could be valued at ~$3M.
• The window: tools cheap, cost near zero, enterprise distracted. Move now or niches get claimed.

metadata.title: The Solo-Founder Playbook: How to Run a $1M ARR SaaS With One Person
metadata.author: ProductLed
metadata.shortDescription:
Most founders believe scaling requires a massive headcount, co-founders, and VC funding. They think success is measured by the size of the team, not the efficiency of the revenue.

In this episode of the ProductLed 100 series, Wes Bush sits down with Vincent Jong (Founder of Poolside Ventures) and Esben Friis-Jensen (Co-Founder of Userflow) to discuss the emerging era of the "One-Person Company" - businesses designed to generate millions in revenue with just a single operator.

Vincent reveals his strategy for building a portfolio of lean, highly profitable SaaS companies like MeetBot. Together with Esben, they break down how AI tools like Lovable and Cursor have removed the technical barrier to entry, why "speed" is the new competitive moat against incumbents like Calendly, and the exact skill sets required to thrive as a solo builder.

Whether you are a developer looking to launch your own venture or a founder trying to maximize efficiency, this episode offers a blueprint for building high-revenue, low-headcount businesses that are built to last forever.

Key Highlights:
01:42: Why Vincent stopped looking for co-founders and started building alone
03:18: The AI Tech Stack: How tools like Lovable and Cursor replace engineering teams
06:22: Why building the product is the easy part (and selling is the hard part)
13:45: Disrupting a Red Ocean: Why MeetBot entered the crowded scheduling market
17:08: The Economics of Infinite Runway: Operating a SaaS for a few hundred dollars a month
20:58: Speed vs. Scale: How one-person teams outmaneuver incumbents
27:54: The "Launch Early" myth vs. the new bar for MVP quality
38:12: Vincent’s advice: Don’t quit your job. Build on weekends

Resources:
📅 MeetBot: The API-first scheduling solution - https://meet.bot
💼 Connect with Vincent Jong on LinkedIn - https://www.linkedin.com/in/vincentjong/
💼 Connect with Wes Bush on LinkedIn - https://www.linkedin.com/in/wesbush/
💼 Connect with Esben Friis-Jensen on LinkedIn - https://www.linkedin.com/in/esbenfriisjensen/
📝 Blog - https://productled.com/blog/the-solo-founder-playbook-how-to-run-a-1m-arr-saas-with-one-person
🧠 Sign up for the ProductLed Newsletter - https://www.productled.com/newsletter

metadata.title: How a Non-Technical Founder Bootstrapped a SaaS to a $3.5M Exit
metadata.author: MicroConf
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you scale a SaaS as a non-technical founder, with no coding skills, no funding, no audience? Spencer Patterson bootstrapped his platform to $140K MRR and sold it for $3.5M, and in this talk he shares the growth tactics that got him there.

📈 SUBSCRIBE: https://www.youtube.com/microconf?sub_confirmation=1
🎟️ JOIN US AT THE NEXT MICROCONF: https://microconf.com/upcoming-events

Spencer Patterson couldn't write a line of code. He hired a 1099 developer to build his MVP (one buggy enough that it shipped with a script to restart the server every few hours) and grew it into a business with a seven-figure exit. 

At MicroConf US 2024 in Atlanta, he breaks down five customer acquisition tactics built for founders who hate traditional outreach, plus the validation questions he'd ask before building anything new.

You'll learn:
▶ Revenue share partnerships that pay for customer acquisition with future dollars, and how 50% lifetime commissions turned affiliates into a first line of defense against churn
▶ Brand ambassador programs built on tracking customer feedback, NPS, and satisfaction data from day one (which also sets up a stronger exit valuation)
▶ Guerrilla marketing: non-automated DMs, pre-built influencer sponsorship contracts, and stealth product placement on Quora and Reddit
▶ Gamification and challenges that reward customers for learning your product, making it stickier without new features
▶ Free tool giveaways (calculators, directories, niche courses) that funnel traffic to your paid product
▶ The validation questions to answer before building. Is it 10x the value of the subscription, and can you reach your audience without ad spend?

Spencer is a bootstrapped SaaS founder who scaled a content platform to $140K MRR as a non-technical solo owner and exited for $3.5M.

This talk was recorded live at MicroConf US 2024: Atlanta.

metadata.title: Bootstrapped SaaS: From $0 to $1M ARR - 3 Times! (Adam Robinson)
metadata.author: SaaS Club
metadata.shortDescription:
Adam Robinson has bootstrapped three separate SaaS companies to over $1M ARR. Here is his repeatable playbook for startup success.

In this episode, Adam (Founder of Retention.com & RB2B) reveals the evolution of his growth strategy across three different decades of SaaS. Learn how he used a "brute force" cold calling strategy to build his first company, the LinkedIn Personal Brand strategy that drove RB2B to $1M ARR in just 16 weeks, and why he believes "Edutainment" is the future of B2B marketing.

🚀 The Serial Playbook: How Adam's time to reach $1M ARR shrunk from 17 months (Company 1) to 16 weeks (Company 3). 
📢 LinkedIn Growth: The "Edutainment" content strategy that grew his following from 0 to 90k+ and fuels his pipeline. 
📧 Cold Email vs. Brand: Why cold outreach is dying and how to replace it with founder-led content. 
📉 The Layoff Lesson: Why cutting his sales team by 75% actually increased efficiency and growth. 
🛠️ The "Free" Wedge: How giving away a valuable product (RB2B) for free created a massive viral loop.

⏱️ Timestamps 
00:00 Introduction & The "Tree" Quote 
03:52 Company 1 (Robly): The "Sweeping Breadcrumbs" Strategy 
07:44 Company 2 (Retention.com): The "Inflammatory Ads" Strategy 
09:17 Company 3 (RB2B): The "Founder Brand" Strategy 
34:25 LinkedIn Playbook: How to Build a Personal Brand from Scratch 
46:42 RB2B Growth: Hitting $1M ARR in 16 Weeks 
49:33 The Hard Thing: Navigating Layoffs & Downsizing

🎧 Full Show Notes: https://saasclub.io/411 
🎤 Subscribe to the Podcast: https://saasclub.io/subscribe 
💌 Get weekly 5-minute SaaS insights https://saasclub.io/email 
💡 Join the SaaS Club founder community: https://saasclub.co/plus

metadata.title: Solo founder, $80M exit, 6 months: The Base44 bootstrapped startup success story | Maor Shlomo
metadata.author: Lenny's Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
Maor Shlomo is the founder of Base44, an AI-powered app builder that he bootstrapped to an over $80 million acquisition by Wix in just six months. As a solo founder (with severe ADHD), he hit $1 million ARR just three weeks after launch and grew the product to more than 400,000 users, all while navigating two wars in Israel and never raising a dollar of outside funding.

*What you’ll learn:*
1. The growth playbook that took Base44 from three friends to 400,000 users without spending any money on marketing
2. How he hasn’t written a single line of front-end code in three months—and how to structure your code repository to make it easier for AI to write your code
3. His AI productivity stack that allowed him to compete against heavily funded competitors
4. Why being a solo founder in AI might be the ultimate advantage (and the wedding story that almost killed the business)
5. The story of signing the $80M acquisition deal while war broke out with Iran
6. How to identify when to sell vs. stay independent (and why Maor chose acquisition despite being highly profitable)
7. The counterintuitive product decision that tripled activation by removing a “helpful” feature
8. How building in public on LinkedIn drove more growth than any paid channel

*Transcript:* https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/the-base44-bootstrapped-startup-success-story-maor-shlomo

*My biggest takeaways (for paid newsletter subscribers):*
https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/i/167384119/my-biggest-takeaways-from-this-conversation

Dscout—The UX platform to capture insights at every stage: from ideation to production: https://www.dscout.com/

*In this episode, we cover:*

metadata.title: How to Recover Failed Payments and Cancellations in B2C SaaS (Full Lifecycle Flow)
metadata.author: RonBuilds
metadata.shortDescription:
Book a call: ronbuilds.dev/book

Most B2C SaaS founders lose six figures a year to bad dunning sequences 
and generic winback emails. Not because the channels don't work, but 
because the flow underneath is wrong.

In this walkthrough I open up the actual decision tree I use to recover 
failed payments and voluntary cancellations for B2C subscription SaaS. 
We diagnose by activation state, route by engagement, treat by channel, 
and measure with proper holdout groups so you actually know what's 
incremental.

If youre running a B2C SaaS between $10M and $25M ARR and your churn 
recovery is built on a generic "Customer.io dunning workflow," this is 
the upgrade.

────────────────────────────────────

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

00:00 Cold open — the two reasons your dunning is broken
01:30 Voluntary vs involuntary cancellations (why the split matters)
03:15 Diagnosing activation state before sending anything
06:00 Activated + engaged: prime them for dunning
09:30 Activated + unengaged: the trap most teams fall into
12:00 Never activated: it's not a dunning problem, it's onboarding
14:45 Paid ad mismatch: when your ad set ≠ app expectation
17:00 Channel choices: in-app, email, retargeting (and the order)
19:00 Holdout groups: how to actually prove recovery is incremental
21:00 The full flow recap + how to deploy it

────────────────────────────────────

WHO I AM

Im Ron, a B2C SaaS lifecycle architect with four years of experience. 
Ive built lifecycle infrastructure and dunning systems for companies like 
Zendrop, Scratch Financial, Ramsey Solutions, and Pickleball.com.

I help B2C SaaS founders lift their exit multiple by architecting 
lifecycle systems on Customer.io, Segment, and Snowflake that drive 
incremental revenue through improved activation, expansion, and retention.

────────────────────────────────────

WANT THIS WIRED UP FOR YOUR SaaS?

Book a call: ronbuilds.dev/book
LinkedIn: linkedin.com/in/ronalddavenport
Twitter: twitter.com/ronbuilds

────────────────────────────────────

#lifecyclemarketing #B2CSaaS #churn #dunning #SaaSretention 
#subscriptionchurn #customerio #lifecyclearchitect #SaaSmarketing 
#winback #churnrecovery #subscriptionrevenue

metadata.title: Stop Losing SaaS Revenue to Failed Payments - 4 Fixes with Dodo Payments
metadata.author: Dodo Payments
metadata.shortDescription:
Failed payment recovery is the cheapest revenue in SaaS — those customers never chose to leave, their card just quietly broke.

A declined renewal, an expired card, a checkout someone wandered away from — that's involuntary churn, not rejection. And unlike winning a new customer, getting this revenue back takes no sales call and no discount war. You just need the recovery layer switched on.

This walkthrough covers the four tools inside Dodo Payments that do it: smart automatic retries that re-attempt fixable declines on the card already on file, subscription dunning emails that walk a customer through replacing a dead card, a manual retry button for when a customer tells you to charge them again right now, and abandoned cart recovery that emails people back to an unfinished checkout with an optional discount.

Then we look at the Analytics tab, where you can see exactly how much revenue came back, which emails converted, and your recovery rate.

Most of this lives under Settings → Recovery and takes a couple of minutes to turn on. If you're running subscriptions and you've never checked your failed renewal rate, start here.

CHAPTERS
0:00 Involuntary churn: the revenue you lose by accident
1:10 Automatic payment retries (and which declines are worth retrying)
2:05 Subscription dunning: emails that recover a dead card
3:00 Manual retry: charging a customer on request
3:50 Abandoned cart recovery for unfinished checkouts
4:40 Tracking recovered revenue in Analytics
5:15 The full safety net, set up once

SETUP GUIDES
Automatic & manual payment retries → go.dodo.pe/payment-retries
Subscription dunning → go.dodo.pe/dunning
Abandoned cart recovery → go.dodo.pe/cart-recovery
Recovery analytics → go.dodo.pe/recovery-analytics

—
Recover failed payments automatically with Dodo Payments → dodopayments.com
Docs & quickstarts → docs.dodopayments.com
Subscribe for more on billing, MoR, and global payments

#saas #involuntarychurn #failedpayments #subscriptionbilling

metadata.title: AskAVC #2 - SaaS Churn: what is it?
metadata.author: Ask a VC
metadata.shortDescription: One of the advantages of SaaS businesses is that you build a customer base that should not only continue to renew over time but also expand if you are delivering value. The opposite is the dreaded revenue churn. What is it and how to measure it is the topic of episode #2 of the #AskAVC channel. You can also check out the blog post based on this video, on my personal website - http://ryanfloyd.org/why-saas-startups-should-care-about-churn/.

segments.text: Hey everybody, Ryan Floyd, managing partner of Storm Ventures here with another video,
part of my video blog series on giving you some advice someone might give you
if I was an investor in your business or on your board or just what you'd like to hear from a venture investor.
Today, we're going to be talking about churn.
I've actually broken it into two part videos.
We'll first talk about churn, what is it,
and then the second part of the video series
we'll talk about what to do about it.
But today we'll talk about the dreaded, the dreaded churn.
You've worked so hard to get all these customers and then they leave and what do you do about it.
So let's get into churn.
So what is churn?
Well, churn simply put is loss of customer revenue.
Some people look at logo churn
and logo churn can be interesting in terms of loss of numbers of customers.
But really, when you look at what impacts your business, certainly in enterprise B2B businesses,
you're really looking at dollar churn in terms of what's really important to be looking at,
because there's probably going to be a variance in customers saying, look, if all customers are exactly
the same amount of revenue that they're paying you, then customer logo churn
and revenue churn will be virtually identical.
But in this case, we're going to be looking at dollar churn and why that's really important.
And the way to sort of think about it in SaaS is that it cuts both ways with these SaaS business models.
The good news is people sign up for subscription and you kind of get these annuity that pays over time,
so long as you're delivering value.
Obviously, the downside is, is if you fail to deliver that value, they have the ability to potentially leave
and with the cloud and APIs and people becoming much more digitally literate, it's getting easier and easier
for many people to decide to move on if they're not getting value out of what you're delivering.
First, let's talk about perspective,
the way to look at churn
is it's really your opportunity to improve.
Another magical thing about SaaS is this constant feedback loop where customers
can leave if they're not getting value.
So I tend to be kind of a glass half full kind of person and so the way I sort of think about churn,
is it's really your ability to improve, improve your processes, your product and everything you're doing
with your customers. And the reality is everybody has churn.
So don't fret because you're going to have periods of high churn and things are going to happen and it's OK
because it happens in every business. But come up from the perspective of, you know,
it's your opportunity to figure out how to do a better a better job in terms of selling.
So there's really, once you move on past logo churn, there's really two kinds of churn to really think about,
gross churn and net churn.
So gross churn is looking at your canceled business
against the ARR over that same period
in terms of what would come up for renewal.
And you might want to look at it over an annualized period over a longer period of time,
because you may only have had some contracts that came up for renewal in a given period,
so looking at monthly numbers, especially if you have a business where people are paying annually in advance,
doesn't make a whole lot of sense.
You need to sometimes look at it more in aggregate or an average number,
a trailing average, things like that.
Just think about really where your churn is headed.
But it's looking at, again, sort of what your overall business is canceling against what your ARR base is.
The other important metric in churn is to think about what's called net churn.
What's different about net churn is net churn takes into account the concept of not only your renewals,
your base, but also your expansion and then also any contractions that you might have had as well.
The reason this is important, especially with respect to the upsells, is that in any SaaS business,
really, one of the, again, things that's magical about SaaS is the compounding nature of SaaS.
And if you're not focused on churn, not only in terms of cancelations, but upsell,

metadata.title: How to Reduce SaaS Churn to 0% (flow revealed)
metadata.author: Vasco Aires
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, I'm sharing exactly how we've significantly reduced churn in our SaaS business. We're consistently hitting four figures daily, so these strategies are proven and tested.

Churn typically occurs when customers feel the value they receive doesn't justify their investment. To combat this, building a genuinely high-quality product is crucial. I discuss the inherent churn differences between B2C and B2B SaaS products, highlighting why B2B usually experiences lower churn due to increased product stickiness. Get more insights into reducing churn for your SaaS here: https://youtu.be/KzRpDczZfWk

You'll learn actionable tips to increase your SaaS product's stickiness by integrating essential features users rely on deeply—like the email automation flows we use. One effective approach we've adopted is adding unique features users lose access to upon canceling, making our SaaS indispensable.

I also detail our carefully designed cancellation flow, aimed at reducing churn and gathering vital user feedback. By encouraging users to schedule a call before canceling, we've successfully identified and resolved key issues, leading to fewer cancellations over time.

A robust cancellation sequence and consistent outreach to former customers have also proven essential in reclaiming churned users and boosting our monthly recurring revenue (MRR).

This video provides practical insights and strategies to lower churn and accelerate your SaaS business growth - after watching it you should have everything you need to reduce your SaaS churn effectively.

🟡 If you're at $0 MRR:
https://everythingsaas.co/ 

🟣 If your MRR is $1K+:
https://vascomonteiro.org/lets-chat/

metadata.author: Churnkey
metadata.shortDescription:
Retention Roundtable - Reducing Involuntary Churn with Payment Recovery

In this video, we dive deep into the world of Failed Payment Recovery — and we’ve got your back 🚀

What You’ll Discover:

Precision Retries: The Game-Changer🎯
- Say hello to Precision Retries—a feature that goes beyond the basics.
- Learn how to toggle it on and let the algorithm work its magic.
- Adaptive scheduling ensures your customer’s card is charged at the most effective times.

Dunning Emails: Nudging Your Way to Success 📧
- Dunning emails are your secret weapon.
- We’ll show you how to craft compelling messages that gently remind customers about failed payments.
- Turn “Oops, your payment failed” into “Hey, let’s fix this together!”

Failed Payment Wall: Breaking Down Barriers 🚧
- Ever heard of a payment wall? It’s like a friendly bouncer for your revenue.
- We’ll explore how to set it up strategically.
- Hint: It’s not about locking customers out; it’s about guiding them back in.

Real-Life Wins and Strategies 💪
- Hear success stories from businesses that turned failed payments into triumphs.
- Get inspired by their tactics and results.
- Spoiler alert: You can do this too!

Join the Retention Revolution

Don’t let those missed payments slip away. Hit play, take notes, and level up your payment recovery game. 💸💡

Follow Us:
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/churnkey/
X: https://x.com/churnkey 
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/churnkey/ 
Learn More or Get Started Fighting Churn:
https://churnkey.co/ 

Don’t forget to subscribe for more content like this! 

#PaymentRecovery #SaaS #Churnkey

The first thing you need to do is make sure that you measure those metrics and be able to slice and dice your churn. Step number two, set up a cancellation process. Now, this isn't always a popular recommendation but in the early days if you truly don't know why customers are canceling and not using your product is not a great enough reason, then you need to avoid the scenario where customers can auto cancel their subscription. I'm not saying make it hard for them, but I am suggesting maybe they email you so you can at least have that conversation about why, what was missing, how could you make the product better and over time you take those responses feed to the product roadmap and then instrument maybe some options they can choose when they self cancel through your product. Three, increase your switching costs. If your product is as easy to switch to as just using another product then it's gonna make it really hard for you to retain your customer. So you gotta start thinking about features that have your users committed to the product. And that can be from a data entry point of view. It could be from a configuration point of view. It can be from a workflow point of view but you need to increase the switching cost to your customers. Four, fix payment failures. If you do not have a specific system for understanding how credit card failure payments or what's called Dunning Management is done at your company, then you're gonna want to look into maybe your credit card provider or services out there that allow you manage that but there is opportunity for you to reduce about 30% of those credit card failure payments that go on to be counted as churn in your business. Five, monitor at risk customers. What does a healthy customer look like? What does one that's about to churn look like from a usage point of view? What features have they been deployed? When are they logging in? There's a bunch of different ways you can set up an instrument, the measurement of is the customer happy? So sitting down, setting that up and then triaging your active users to your customer support team, your customer success is a really important way to reduce your churn in your SaaS business. To quickly recap, one, instrument your metrics. Two, set up a cancellation process. Three, increase your switching costs. Four, fix your payment failures. Five, monitor at risk customers. metadata.title: SaaS Churn Prediction: How to Predict Churn Before Renewal
metadata.author: Gamify Data
metadata.shortDescription:
SaaS churn prediction gives every account a chance of leaving within a set window, scored months before renewal. Here is how to set it up so your customer success team can actually work from it: agree on one definition of churn, fix the scoring window, build every input as of the score date, check that the probabilities mean what they say, and test on renewals the model never saw. Then compare it with the simple rule you already use.

Read the full post: https://gamifydata.com/insights/saas-churn-prediction

metadata.title: SaaS Competitor Comparison Pages: Why you NEED to Build them
metadata.author: Rock The Rankings: B2B SaaS GEO & SEO Agency
metadata.shortDescription:
Competitor comparison landing pages are a classic SaaS strategy to drive bottom-of-the-funnel traffic and conversions when prospects are in the transactional intent phase of the marketing funnel.

These pages are crucial for helping your customers to understand whether they’re really the right fit for your service, or not – and are an extremely effective way to hone in on your ideal customer, rather than simply adding customers that will eventually churn.

Many SaaS organizations either:

- Neglect creating these pages all together as they find it unethical to say anything that could shed the competition in a negative light
Create these pages, but haven’t really gone about it in the best way possible (i.e. it’s all about “us, us, us.” or beating up the competition)

-Competitor comparison landing pages have become almost essential at this point in order to not allow your competitors to control the conversation on how their product stacks up against yours.

These pages can also be extremely effective for young SaaS startups with little brand recognition, and minimal search traffic.

Use our best practice guide and template to get started: https://www.rocktherankings.com/competitor-comparison-landing-pages/

In AI search, Constant Hire became ChatGPT's #1 recommendation and brought in $70,000 in four months, and Penn Tool's revenue from ChatGPT grew 12x in ten months. Pricing from $5,000/month, no multi-year contracts.
2. Rock The Rankings: B2B SaaS only, 300+ SaaS engagements, founder-led by Justin Berg (in SEO since 2007). Starts most clients with a 90-day program and credits AI search for demos by matching CRM data with "how did you hear about us" answers. Strategy from $5,000/month; full program $7,500 to $15,000+/month. Built for Series A to C companies.
3. First Page Sage: 17 years in B2B SaaS, its largest client group, with 200+ SaaS clients served. Month-to-month engagements with 6 to 7 deliverables a month; published GEO pricing of $6,000 to $12,000/month. Positions itself as a premium agency.
4. Optimist: GEO and SEO consultancy for B2B tech, with clients like Semrush, ZoomInfo and Superhuman. Says its work grew AI referral revenue 49x over 14 months for one B2B tech client. Strategy projects from $2,500; ongoing advising from $3,000/month.
 
HOW WE RANKED THEM
Main factor: results getting software companies more demos, trials and pipeline from Google and AI search, not traffic or rankings alone. Second factor: pricing.
 
HOW GEO WORKS FOR SAAS COMPANIES
Software buyers already ask AI. In G2's 2026 survey of 1,000+ B2B software buyers, 82% had gotten software recommendations from an AI tool in the last two years, and half said AI mattered most when narrowing down and comparing options. Review sites (38%) and AI tools (37%) are now the two biggest influences on a shortlist.
For "best employee scheduling software", Google's AI answer cited Zapier's "best of" list, one vendor's own page, Reddit threads and six YouTube videos: 6 of its 8 sources were videos.
Four things get your software picked:
1. Pages that match how buyers ask: category, use case, industry and comparison/alternatives pages, each with pricing info and an FAQ
2. Mentions where buyers and AI look: "best of" software lists, G2 and Capterra, industry publications, Reddit and YouTube
3. Consistent product facts: the same positioning, pricing and features on your site, review profiles and listings, with schema markup
4. Specifics: a 2024 Princeton study found that adding statistics and cited sources raised visibility in AI answers by up to 40%
SEO and GEO belong together: AI tools lean on what already ranks on Google. Zapier's list ranks on the first page of Google for that scheduling search, and it's the first source the AI answer cites.
 
4 QUESTIONS TO ASK ANY AGENCY
1. Which buyer prompts will you track, by category, use case and competitor?
2. How will you tie AI search to demos and pipeline in our CRM? Most AI-referred buyers show up as "direct" traffic.
3. Which sites will you get us mentioned on? Real names.
4. Who builds the strategy: a senior person who knows software buyers, or a template?
 
Made by 95 Projects. Competitor details come from public sources and the agencies' own claims. Narration is AI-generated.

metadata.title: B2B SaaS comparison pages: The COMPLETE guide for marketers & founders
metadata.author: Josh Gallant
metadata.shortDescription:
What if every prospect in your space came directly to YOU for advice on which product to use?

In this video I explain the power of comparison pages in B2B SaaS, why they're crucial for startups, how to overcome common hesitations, how to measure their ROI, and the key elements of an effective B2B SaaS comparison page.

0:00 - 0:17 Intro
0:17 - 2:35 Why comparison pages matter
2:35 - 8:18 Common hesitations (and why to ignore them)
8:18 - 15:25 ROI of comparison pages
15:25 - 16:01 Anatomy of a comparison page
16:01 - 19:00 1) SEO details
19:00 - 20:38 2) Above the fold
20:38 - 24:00 3) Feature tables
24:00 - 26:15 4) Qualitative differentiators
26:15 - 28:58 5) When to pick them
28:58 - 32:51 6) Social proof
32:51 - 34:24 7) Relevant FAQs
34:24 - 35:00 8) High contrast CTA
35:00 - 38:02 Final thoughts on SaaS comparison pages

metadata.title: How to Win Customers From Bigger Competitors: 5 SaaS Playbooks
metadata.author: MicroConf
metadata.shortDescription:
How to win customers from bigger competitors: five competitor marketing playbooks for bootstrapped SaaS founders who can't outspend anyone.

📈 SUBSCRIBE: https://www.youtube.com/@MicroConf?sub_confirmation=1
🎟️ JOIN US AT THE NEXT MICROCONF: https://microconf.com/upcoming-events

Big B2B SaaS companies are losing customers, and those customers aren't going back to spreadsheets and email. Dev Basu (at MicroConf US 2023 in Denver, CO) argues bootstrapped founders have one real advantage — clock speed — for picking up accounts their largest competitor can no longer keep. Rather than building brand awareness you can't afford, he shows how to slip into consideration midstream and reach buyers at the moment they're already frustrated with what they're using. 

Five playbooks, drawn from his agency's work with over 100 B2B SaaS companies, most set up in about a day.

00:00 The edge bootstrapped founders have: clock speed
02:57 Why the 800-pound gorilla feels unbeatable
03:56 Three things holding bootstrapped SaaS back
10:21 What if your marketing were as engineered as your software?
11:34 Three mistakes: "that channel doesn't work for us"
16:42 Five playbooks
16:53 Case study: how Rally won HubSpot and Porsche
19:03 Defining "better": cost-effective, flexible, less risky
22:17 Slipping into consideration midstream
25:23 Upgraders vs. switchers
26:24 Playbook 1: Competitor comparison pages
32:20 Playbook 2: $10/day Google Discovery ads
37:08 Playbook 3: Comment on their coattails
39:15 Playbook 4: Pick on their price increases
40:17 Playbook 5: Flex your flexibility
42:52 Q&A: where comparison pages belong, and selling the demo

What you'll learn:

- Comparison pages that convert — why feature-for-feature checkbox tables lose, and why crediting your competitor sells better
- Review sites as a copy source: mine complaints on your competitor's Capterra and GetApp listings, then answer them
- Google Discovery ads on $10/day, targeted at Gmail renewal notices, competitor pages, and high-intent software categories
- Upgraders vs. switchers: the two dissatisfied audiences already hunting for an alternative
- Price hikes and product sunsets tracked with free Google Alerts — and the response Nathan Barry ran against ActiveCampaign
- Flexibility big companies can't match: free concierge onboarding with qualification rules, white-glove service, founder visibility

Dev Basu is founder and CEO of Powered by Search, a B2B SaaS marketing agency working with over 100 B2B SaaS companies, and a TinySeed mentor.

This talk was recorded live at MicroConf US 2023: Denver.

Micro SaaS apps are compact software solutions that cater to specific needs or tasks, offering a more focused and targeted approach compared to traditional software applications. Unlike bulky and complex programs, micro SaaS apps are lightweight, easy to use, and often customizable to suit individual preferences. This makes them ideal for enhancing productivity and efficiency in various work environments.

Chrome extensions play a crucial role in enhancing workflow and simplifying tasks for users.
