metadata.title: PROFITABLE CHROME EXTENSION BLUEPRINT | Build And Scale Micro Tools For Passive Monthly Revenue
metadata.author: W3 NOTES | The Internet Cash Flow Library
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to build and scale **profitable Chrome extensions** for **passive monthly revenue** with this comprehensive blueprint. Chrome extensions represent a massive, underutilized digital economy, reaching over **3 billion users** through the Chrome Web Store. This video breaks down the exact system to go from zero to a portfolio of micro-tools that function as a **Micro SaaS embedded directly into the user's browser**.


**WHY CHROME EXTENSIONS?**

Unlike traditional SaaS platforms, extensions intercept existing attention by living inside a user's daily workflow. They require **minimal infrastructure**, can be built by solo developers using familiar web technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript), and offer free global distribution. In 2026, AI coding assistants have reduced build times by up to **70%**, allowing founders to ship MVPs in days rather than months. The broader extension market has reached approximately **$7.8 billion**, with segments like AI-powered tools exploding at a 22.5% CAGR.


**THE PROFITABLE NICHE MINING SYSTEM**

Success starts with finding **repetitive browser friction** rather than "cool" ideas. Focus on **utility over spectacle** in high-value niches:
*   **B2B Workflow Automation:** Filling micro-feature gaps in apps like Salesforce, Trello, or Gmail.
*   **Data Extraction & Scraping:** Tools for professionals to stop manual copying and pasting.
*   **AI-Native Enhancers:** Summarizers, prompt libraries, and writing assistants that leverage the generative AI boom.
*   **Developer & Creator Tools:** Specialized tools for CSS inspection, JSON formatting, or content analysis.


**VALIDATION & BUILDING FAST**

Don't build in a vacuum. Use the **30-day validation framework**: talk to users in niche communities (Reddit, Discord) and measure interest via "fake door" landing pages before writing code. When building, always use **Manifest V3 (MV3)**, the modern standard required by Google. To speed up development, leverage production-ready boilerplates like **Plasmo, WXT, or CRXJS** to handle authentication, payments, and deployment tooling.


**ORGANIC GROWTH (0 TO 1,000 USERS)**

Ditch paid ads. The most sustainable path to 1,000 users is **organic growth**:
*   **Chrome Web Store SEO (ASO):** Use keyword-rich titles and outcome-based descriptions to dominate search intent.
*   **Visual Conversion:** High-quality annotated screenshots and sub-30-second demo videos act as your primary sales page.
*   **Product-Led Growth (PLG) Loops:** Design features that encourage users to invite colleagues or leave reviews after a "win".


**MONETIZATION MODELS THAT WORK**

*   **Freemium (The Indie Default):** Offer a genuinely useful free tier and gate advanced features or usage limits behind a paywall. Typical conversion rates range from 2–5%.
*   **Subscriptions:** Best for AI-powered or ongoing service tools, generating predictable monthly recurring revenue (MRR).
*   **One-Time / Lifetime Deals (LTDs):** Great for simple utilities and upfront cash injections on platforms like AppSumo.
*   **Stripe & ExtensionPay:** Since native Web Store payments were deprecated, these are the standard tools for handling billing and licensing.


**SCALING TO AN EXIT**

A single extension can provide a side income of **$500–$2,000/month**, while top performers like **GMass** ($130k/mo) or **Closet Tools** ($42k/mo) reach massive scale. Treat extensions as a **portfolio business**—stack multiple micro-tools to compound revenue and reduce risk. When ready, these extensions are highly sellable digital assets on marketplaces like **Acquire.com or Flippa**, typically fetching **2x to 4x annual revenue**.


**RESOURCES MENTIONED:**

*   **Boilerplates:** Plasmo, WXT, CRXJS, ShipFast.
*   **Payment Handlers:** Stripe, ExtensionPay, Lemon Squeezy.
*   **AI Tools:** Claude, Cursor, Lovable.dev.

Whether you're a seasoned developer or a "vibe coder" using AI, the browser is the next operating system for micro-SaaS. **Build once, earn forever**.

**Subscribe for more insights on building digital assets and passive income systems!**

metadata.title: How I Invest in Startups From an Island (Real TrustMRR Deal)
metadata.author: Startup Island
metadata.shortDescription:
I went startup shopping on TrustMRR, not vibe-coding from zero with no customers.

This episode is a full walkthrough of UltraWideo (browser extension that removes black bars and fills the screen): verified revenue, asking price, T30 vs MRR multiples, Chrome Web Store user numbers, free vs Pro pricing, and the exact opening offer I’d make.

Not investment advice. Not financial advice. Not a recommendation that you buy anything.  
I’m documenting what I would do myself. Do your own diligence.

UltraWideo listing: https://trustmrr.com/startup/ultrawideo?ref=jack-malinowski-be3b02

In this video:
- Why TrustMRR is different (payment-provider verified revenue)
- Asking price $13k (down from $15k)
- Why T30 multiple (~1.9x) is not the multiple I’d underwrite
- Why I’d price off MRR instead (~$343) and what that does to payback
- What the product actually is (Chrome/Firefox extension)
- How to read CWS “users” vs weekly actives (I show my own extension dashboard)
- What I’d demand from the seller before wiring money
- Free vs Pro (~$30/year ≈ $2.50/mo) and ~129 subscribers
- My starting offer math: MRR × 12 × 2.5 ≈ $10,290 → I’d open at $10,000

Timestamps:
0:00 Startup shopping (not building from scratch)
0:22 Disclaimer: not investment / financial advice
0:39 TrustMRR: verified Stripe/payment revenue
1:15 What I’m shopping for (stable, paying, for sale)
1:31 Deal focus: UltraWideo
1:40 Last 30 days revenue ($570) and why simple valuation fails
2:01 Asking price $13,000 (was $15,000)
2:20 Calculator: ask ÷ T30 ÷ 12 ≈ 1.9x multiple
2:54 Payback story on T30 math (and why it’s incomplete)
3:00 Better lens: ask ÷ MRR ($343) ÷ 12 ≈ 3x+
3:35 What UltraWideo does (site / promise)
4:32 Why I don’t need to “fall in love” with the UI to underwrite
5:08 Chrome Web Store reality (lives in the browser)
5:33 CWS listing + demo video
5:47 ~80,000 users on the store page
6:03 How CWS numbers actually work (my Mobile Simulator dashboard)
6:25 Weekly unique users vs public “users” count
7:04 Daily users, enabled rate, what I’d request pre-deal
7:41 Installs, uninstalls, impressions (Search / ChatGPT sources)
8:01 Back to UltraWideo: 80k is a real Google number
8:14 Reviews (~600, ~4.3) and what you can/can’t fake
8:33 EU Trader badge / DUNS and why monetization legality matters
9:10 80k users ≠ 80k paying customers
9:26 Free vs Pro features and pricing
9:35 Pro ~$30/year ≈ ~$2.50/month
9:53 ~129 subscribers vs listed MRR
10:15 My offer formula: $343 MRR × 12 × 2.5
10:34 ≈ $10,290 → opening offer $10,000 (~80% of ask)
10:58 Next steps offline + more listings coming
11:14 CTA + outro (Startup Island)

If it’s still for sale, link is above. Next episodes: more listings and how I look at projects before putting money in.

#TrustMRR #SaaS #ChromeExtension #MicroSaaS #Acquisitions #StartupShopping #BuyAndBuild

metadata.shortDescription:
How Shopify subscriptions work and what they give your e-commerce store: recurring revenue, easier planning and loyal customers, with native Shopify Subscriptions instead of a third-party app.

I explain selling plan groups, selling plans and subscription contracts in plain words, then show a real candy box subscription I built on a Shopify Hydrogen store: build-your-own box, subscription checkout, orders and contracts in the admin, and a customer account where people skip, pause or cancel. At the end, my take on when native subscriptions are enough and when you need custom work. No coding tutorial, just how it works for the business.

Part 2: Why Your Store Never Matches Your Figma → https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qMrM2LTTFPI

metadata.title: Micro SaaS on Shopify: Your Path to Success!
metadata.author: MicroSaaS
metadata.shortDescription:
In today's fast-paced digital world, the concept of micro SaaS apps on platforms like Shopify has been gaining significant traction. As a developer looking to carve out a successful niche in the micro SaaS business landscape, understanding the nuances of this emerging trend is crucial.

Micro SaaS apps, which are typically small focused software solutions catering to specific niche markets, offer immense potential in the current digital landscape. These apps provide businesses with cost-effective and customizable solutions to streamline their operations, enhance customer experiences, and drive growth for entrepreneurs.

Micro SaaS apps present a unique opportunity to tap into underserved markets, build recurring revenue streams, and establish a loyal customer base. However, while the micro SaaS space holds great promise, it also comes with its own set of challenges. Entrepreneurs need to navigate competition, market saturation, and evolving customer demands.

To succeed in this dynamic environment, identifying unmet needs and leveraging innovative technologies are essential. By delivering exceptional value through their micro SaaS app on Shopify platform developers can overcome these challenges and thrive in the micro SaaS ecosystem.

Understanding the process involved from ideation and market research to development testing and marketing plays a crucial role in bringing a successful micro SaaS app to market. By leveraging Shopify's robust platform developers can create scalable user-friendly solutions that resonate with their target audience and drive business growth.

metadata.title: From $80K to $418K: How Carlos Flipped a Shopify App into a Life-Changing Exit
metadata.author: Rags to Riches
metadata.shortDescription:
Carlos was just a support rep when he stumbled onto an $80K Shopify app on Acquire.com. With only $12K down and a creative financing stack, he scaled CartSaver Pro from $4,200 to $8,700 in monthly recurring revenue. Eighteen months later, he sold it for $418K—netting $280K after debt payoff.
This video breaks down the deal terms, growth playbook, and exit strategy that turned a side hustle into life-changing cash. If you’ve ever wondered how micro-SaaS acquisitions can outpace a 9–5 salary, this story is your roadmap.


What if one late-night crash at work changed the entire course of your life? That’s exactly what happened to Carlos, a customer support rep who turned flash-sale chaos into a six-figure exit.

In this video, you’ll see how Carlos discovered an $80K Shopify app listed on Acquire.com, structured a creative financing stack, and scaled it from $4,200 to $8,700 in monthly recurring revenue. Eighteen months later, he sold it to a roll-up fund for $418K all-cash, netting $280K after clearing loans and notes.

We’ll break down step-by-step:

- Why Shopify apps are hidden gold mines
- How to finance acquisitions with minimal personal cash
- The 90-day plan that doubled value with simple UI + pricing tweaks
- What made this app irresistible to acquirers

This isn’t just a success story, it’s a roadmap for anyone looking to escape the grind through micro-SaaS acquisitions.

📅 New videos every Tuesday and Thursday — real-world deal stories, playbooks for flipping digital assets, and practical strategies for building freedom.

👉 Subscribe now so you don’t miss the next acquisition story.
📩 Have you ever thought about buying a “boring” app or online business? Drop your story in the comments!

#ShopifyApp #MicroSaaS #AcquireDotCom #DigitalAssets #PassiveIncome #CarlosSuccessStory

segments.text: Carlos had been working in e-commerce
customer support for years. And if there
was one thing he knew for certain, it
was that flash sales were both a
blessing and a curse. They brought
traffic, yes, but they also brought
chaos. Every time a big discount event
rolled out, the store servers would
strain, pages would freeze, carts would
crash, and customers would flood in with
angry messages. His days would often
stretch late into the night,
troubleshooting abandoned cart issues
and soothing frustrated shoppers. But
one night, while wrestling with yet
another mess after a flash sale
meltdown, Carlos's mind wandered to a
simple but curious thought. Who actually
owned the little apps that kept these
online stores running? The answer came
to him not through a colleague or a tech
blog, but through a late night browsing
session on acquire.com.
What began as idle curiosity quickly
became something more. He scrolled
through listings of digital products for
sale. And that's when he saw it. a
modest Shopify app called CartSaver Pro
with a listing price of $80,000.
It didn't look flashy. There was no
hyped up marketing, no screaming
headlines about explosive growth, just a
straightforward pitch, an app built to
help online stores recover abandoned
carts. He knew from experience that this
was a real pain point in e-commerce. The
description mentioned it had 450 paying
stores and generated $4,200 in monthly
recurring revenue. Carlos' mind started
turning. Why a Shopify app? For one,
Shopify's platform had over 2 million
merchants, and getting them to install
an app was often just a one-click
process. For another, the billing was
usage based, meaning revenue scaled
automatically as the merchants
themselves grew. And unlike selling
physical goods, which involved inventory
headaches, customer returns, and
shipping logistics, running an app could
mean relatively low maintenance, often
just a few lines of code to update, and
occasional customer support tickets to
resolve. Carlos dug deeper into the
listing. The seller was Steve, a
62-year-old man who had built CartSaver
Pro originally to help his daughter's
small boutique shop. Now semi-retired
and more interested in woodworking than
coding, Steve had decided to list the
app for sale. The problem, it had been
sitting on the market for 6 months
without a single serious offer. Carlos
was intrigued but cautious. The price,
$80,000, wasn't exactly pocket change.
Still, something about it felt like an
overlooked opportunity. He could see the
cracks where value was leaking and he
imagined how a few strategic moves might
turn this unpolished app into a much
more profitable venture. Negotiations
started and soon they were talking
numbers. They settled on a deal
structure that minimized Carlos's
personal cash risk. Out of the $80,000
price tag, Carlos would put down just
$12,000 in cash, 15%. Steve agreed to
carry a $28,000 seller note at 7%
interest to be paid over 3 years. The
remaining $40,000 would come from a
revenue-based loan at 9% APR with
repayments tied to 15% of the app's
future monthly recurring revenue. It was
a creative capital stack that allowed
Carlos to keep most of his cash free
while still securing the business.
Before finalizing, Carlos conducted
thorough due diligence. He reviewed
Stripe exports and liked what he saw.
monthly churn was only 2.9% and net
revenue retention was a healthy 106%
meaning the app was not only holding on
to customers but growing revenue from
the existing base. He paid 1,000 for a
GitHub code audit which came back
positive. The app used a modern tech
stack and there was no significant
technical debt lurking in the
background. Customer support seemed
manageable too with only about four
tickets per week. Carlos wasn't just
buying the app, he had a plan. His
90-day value ad road map was aggressive
but realistic. First, he invested in a
UI refresh. He found a designer on
Fiverr to modernize the look and feel of
the app, improving onboarding flow and
user experience. The result, onboarding
conversions increased by 18% almost
overnight. Next, he introduced tiered
pricing. Until then, the app had a
single flat rate plan. Carlos launched a
new $29 per month growth plan, adding an
AB testing widget as the premium
feature. Finally, he rolled out an
affiliate program with a generous 30%
recurring payout, which attracted
influencers and consultants in the
e-commerce space. In just the first
month, this brought in 120 new installs.
By the 12-month mark, the numbers told a
very different story than the one Steve
had tried to sell for half a year
without success. Monthly recurring
revenue had more than doubled, reaching
Churn had dropped to 1.8% and Carlos was
spending only about 10 hours a week on
the business, mostly on roadmap planning
and partner calls. rather than
firefighting. The operation was lean,
efficient, and steadily growing. Then,
in the 18th month, an email landed in
his inbox that made him stop and stare.
It was from a Shopify app roll-up fund.
They were making acquisition offers and
had noticed CartSaver Pro's recent
growth. The offer was straightforward,
all cash for the app. Carlos ran the
numbers. The loan would be paid off, the
seller note settled, and after all
obligations, he would net roughly
He thought about the $12,000 in cash he
had initially put in and realized the
return on investment was extraordinary.
Without hesitation, he accepted the
offer. Looking back, Carlos saw the
journey as a textbook example of how
MicroSASS could outperform a traditional
salaried job. Not just in income
potential, but in flexibility and
control over one's time. By structuring
the deal creatively, he had protected
his personal cash while still taking
ownership of an asset. And by making
relatively small changes, refreshing the
UI, tweaking pricing, and introducing an
affiliate program, he had managed to
more than double the app's value in
under two years. What's striking about
Carlos's story is how it upends the myth
that big wins in tech require building
the next unicorn startup from scratch.
Here was a small overlooked app with
modest revenue, ignored by other buyers,
sitting quietly in a marketplace until
the right person saw its potential. He
didn't invent anything groundbreaking.
He simply bought something
underappreciated and made it better. And
in doing so, he turned a deal that no
one else wanted into a six-figure
payday. If you strip away the details,
the principles are almost boring in
their simplicity. First, look for
markets with built-in demand and low
friction for customer adoption.
Shopify's ecosystem with millions of
merchants in a one-click install process
checked that box perfectly. Second,
leverage deal structures that allow you
to keep most of your cash intact while
using the asset's own revenue to fund
its purchase. Third, identify small but
high impact improvements, whether in
product design, pricing, or marketing,
that can compound growth. And finally,
know your exit strategy from day one.
Carlos didn't buy CartSaver Pro without
thinking about how and when he might
sell it. Of course, not every
acquisition works out like this. The
story could have gone very differently
if churn had been high, the code base a
mess, or if the app had been in a
shrinking niche. But Carlos did his
homework. He validated that the product
solved a real problem, that the existing
customer base was loyal, and that there
was room to grow. In the end, his
success wasn't about luck. It was about
spotting value where others didn't
bother to look and having the confidence
to act on it. Stories like these are a
reminder that opportunity doesn't always
announce itself with neon signs and
viral buzz. Sometimes it's tucked away
in the quiet corners of an online
marketplace, wearing the digital
equivalent of an unremarkable sweater.
All it takes is one person to recognize
what's underneath, to see the gold in
something others have overlooked.
Carlos' journey with CartSaver Pro is
proof that with a sharp eye, a smart
plan, and the willingness to execute,
even the most unassuming deal can turn
into a gamecher. So the next time you're
browsing listings for digital businesses
or even just idally scrolling through
side hustle ideas, remember this story.
Somewhere in that endless stream of
opportunities could be the thing that
changes your financial trajectory. It
might not look glamorous. It might have
sat there for months without a bite, but
if you can see what others can't, if you
can imagine the small changes that will
make a big difference, then you just
might be the next person to turn an
$80,000 overlooked asset into a $418,000
cash out. And if that thought excites
you, it might be worth asking yourself,
what's stopping you from finding your
own CartSaver Pro?

**💡 Quiet Empires: The Surprising Power of “Microsoftware” for Recurring Revenue Success**

What if we told you that the most profitable online businesses in 2025 aren’t massive startups, but tiny, laser-focused tools built to solve annoyingly specific problems? In today’s episode, we unpack the powerful idea of **“Microsoftware as a Service”** — or “Microsofts” — a counterintuitive business model quietly powering a new wave of solo entrepreneurs, indie hackers, and digital creators.

We’re talking about solving hyper-niche pain points with simple software — tools that might only serve 100 to 200 people, yet generate thousands in monthly recurring revenue. Whether it’s real estate agents needing auto-formatted Instagram stories, Shopify owners tracking review scores, or podcasters automating post-production — these microtools are flipping the startup game on its head. And the best part? You don’t even need to know how to code.

In this episode, you’ll learn how this quiet model works, why it thrives without VC funding, and how YOU can start building your own digital mini-empire using no-code tools and AI-powered APIs. We dive into the mindset shift, the tech enablers, and the types of “pebble-in-the-shoe” problems worth solving in this new micro-era of entrepreneurship.

---

### 🔍 What You’ll Learn:

* The definition and philosophy behind “Microsoftware as a Service”
* Real-world examples of profitable microtools
* Why niche is more powerful than scale in 2025
* How no-code/low-code platforms are breaking barriers
* Ways to identify high-value micro-problems
* How to build recurring revenue without chasing virality or VC money

---

### 🕒 Timestamps:

* 00:00 – The rise of quiet, niche-focused businesses
* 00:32 – What “Microsoftware” really means
* 01:02 – Solving ultra-specific problems
* 01:33 – Why big companies ignore these pain points
* 02:01 – Real examples: Real estate agents, podcasters, Shopify
* 03:00 – The mechanics: small user base, big returns
* 03:31 – Recurring revenue from just a few hundred customers
* 04:02 – No-code and APIs: the new builder’s toolkit
* 04:31 – Adding AI without being an engineer
* 05:00 – The mindset shift: solve the small problems
* 05:28 – Quiet Empires: sustainable, focused, profitable

---

👍 If this video gave you a new perspective on business and money-making in 2025, hit that **LIKE** button, **SUBSCRIBE** for more eye-opening strategies, and drop a comment: *What's one tiny problem you'd love to see solved by a microtool?*

---

\#microstartups #recurringrevenue #nocodebusiness #quietwealth

metadata.shortDescription:
Erikas runs 5 different Shopify apps, making $4.5M/Year. In this interview, he breaks down the simple playbook behind his explosive growth. And how he went from $2/hour to making millions with 90% margins. 

Interested in building a business like Erikas? Learn more here → https://go.starterstory.com/mondayerikas

52 micro startup ideas → https://www.starterstory.com/micro?utm_source=youtube&utm_campaign=erikas

Follow Erika's journey:
🎥   https://x.com/malisauskasLT

🔔 Follow the Second Channel: @StarterStoryBuild 
🏁 We're hiring: starterstory.com/jobs

Chapters:
0:00 - Intro
1:33 - Breakdown of Apps
2:16 - Building apps on platforms
4:40 - How to find winning ideas
6:33 - An under-the-radar marketplace to build on
8:37 - His process for building apps
11:11 - The strategy that changed everything
13:32 - 3 step launch strategy
14:12 - Tech stack
15:17 - Day in the life
16:13 - Advice to new founders

metadata.title: How We Built 10 Shopify Apps Used by 250,000+ Merchants | Justas Galaburda
metadata.author: The SaaS Hub - The Shopify Podcast
metadata.shortDescription:
How do you build not just one successful Shopify app—but an entire portfolio used by more than 250,000 merchants?

In this episode of The SaaS Hub Shopify Podcast, I sit down with Justas Galaburda, Co-founder of Essential Apps, to discuss what it takes to build multiple category-leading Shopify apps, scale a product portfolio, and create long-term businesses inside the Shopify ecosystem.

Before founding Essential Apps, Justas co-founded Oberlo, one of Shopify's most influential dropshipping apps, which was later acquired by Shopify. After the acquisition, he spent several years at Shopify before starting Essential Apps in 2022.

Today, Essential Apps has built a portfolio of 10+ Shopify apps, all focused on solving everyday merchant problems. Collectively, their apps are trusted by 250,000+ Shopify merchants, with multiple apps carrying the Built for Shopify badge and maintaining outstanding 5-star ratings.

This conversation goes far beyond product features. We dive into the mindset behind building successful Shopify apps, identifying market opportunities, scaling product teams, and how the Shopify ecosystem continues to evolve.

In this episode, we cover:

✅ Building Oberlo and what it was like being acquired by Shopify

✅ Lessons learned from working inside Shopify

✅ Why Essential Apps chose a portfolio strategy instead of building one flagship product

✅ How they decide which Shopify app to build next

✅ Building products that consistently earn 5-star reviews

✅ The importance of the Built for Shopify program

✅ Scaling to 250,000+ merchants across multiple apps

✅ Why solving simple merchant problems often wins

✅ AI-generated apps and the future of Shopify development

✅ Shopify App Store competition and discovery challenges

✅ Advice for founders building Shopify apps today

Whether you're a Shopify app founder, merchant, agency, SaaS builder, or entrepreneur, this episode offers practical insights into product strategy, execution, and building businesses that stand the test of time.

👤 Guest

Justas Galaburda
Co-founder, Essential Apps

Essential Apps builds one of the largest portfolios of Shopify applications, helping more than 250,000 merchants improve conversions, increase AOV, optimize storefronts, and grow their businesses.

Their portfolio includes:

• Essential Countdown Timer Bar
• Essential Announcement Bar
• Essential Trust Badges & Icons
• Essential Free Shipping Upsell
• Essential Cart Drawer & Upsell
• Essential Preorder & Back in Stock
• Essential Loyalty Program
• Essential Estimated Delivery Date
• Essential AI SEO
• Essential CRO Split Testing

Explore their apps:
https://apps.shopify.com/partners/essentials25

🤝 Episode Sponsor

This episode is proudly supported by The Support Heroes.

If you're building a Shopify app and want to provide exceptional customer support without building an in-house team, The Support Heroes helps app founders deliver fast, knowledgeable, and human support that scales alongside their business.

🌐 https://www.thesupportheroes.com/

🚀 About The SaaS Hub

The SaaS Hub helps Shopify merchants discover the best apps, compare solutions, and build the right technology stack for their stores.

Through in-depth founder interviews, app reviews, merchant resources, and ecosystem insights, we aim to help everyone in the Shopify community make better technology decisions.

🌐 https://thesaashub.com/

🔗 Connect with Justas

LinkedIn:
https://www.linkedin.com/in/justas-galaburda-82882056/

Essential Apps:
https://apps.shopify.com/partners/essentials25

If you enjoyed this conversation, don't forget to Like, Subscribe, and share it with another Shopify founder, merchant, or ecommerce operator.

Every week on The SaaS Hub Shopify Podcast, we bring you conversations with the founders, operators, and leaders shaping the Shopify ecosystem.

metadata.title: From Tech Lead to SaaS Founder: Why I’m Starting with a Shopify App
metadata.author: ThomSaaS Builder
metadata.shortDescription:
I’m Thomas, a Tech Lead and Full Stack TypeScript Engineer working mainly with Next.js, NestJS and microservice architectures.

In this first episode, I explain why I’m starting this channel, why I want to build a SaaS product in public, and why I’ve chosen to begin with a B2B Shopify app.

This project has several goals:

• Build a real product that demonstrates my technical skills
• Create new opportunities for freelance work or international roles
• Learn market research, customer discovery, positioning and pricing
• Test whether a side project can eventually become a sustainable software business

I also explain why I’m focusing on B2B rather than B2C, and why ecosystem-based products such as Shopify apps, WordPress plugins or platform add-ons can be a practical starting point for a first bootstrapped SaaS.

Instead of spending months building an entirely new product with no proven demand, my approach will be to study existing markets, analyse competitors already generating revenue, identify real customer problems and build a focused solution.

In the next episode, I’ll start researching Shopify app opportunities and narrowing down the type of product I want to build.

No overnight-success promises. No fake revenue screenshots. Just the real process of researching, building, launching and learning in public.

Subscribe to follow the journey from idea to first customers.

#SaaS #ShopifyApps #BuildInPublic #B2BSaaS #SoftwareEngineering #IndieHacker

The last argument would be that generally these are quick products to build. You can test and iterate quickly and I don't necessarily need to build a SaaS for months in my cave before realizing that actually there are no clients for this need. Of course, Shopify isn't the only platform that allows independent developers to set up an app on their platform and build through their marketplace. There are WordPress plugins, apps on monday.com or even Heroku. But because of my background, I have an affinity for Shopify. Though in the future, why not create software on other platforms? We'll see. So that's roughly the direction I'm going to take next. A mostly B2B oriented SaaS tied to the Shopify platform. So next, I'm going to do some research because right now I just have a vague direction, but roughly the path is starting to take shape. I've simply explained the type of application I'm going to create and why. And in the next video, I'll get back to you with much more specific details about the app I want to build. But I'll tell you in advance, I'm not going to reinvent the wheel. I'll probably target existing markets with competitors who already have revenue, which proves to me that there are indeed people willing to pay to solve the kind of problem my competitors are already solving. To be honest, I don't want to play the innovator because often those innovative projects with zero competitors turn into total flops with zero revenue, zero traction, zero clients. So there you go. I've already teased the next episode a bit. Take care and see you next time.

metadata.title: How to Grow a Micro SaaS to $30,000 MRR on the Shopify App Store
metadata.author: hexdevs
metadata.shortDescription:
Learn how to start and grow a Shopify Micro SaaS to $30,000 MRR and more than 20,000 users in about 14 months with Preetam Nath and Sankalp Jonna, co-founders of DelightChat.

Highlights:

- How to do market research before writing any line of code and how being a little "impatient" with growth is a good thing for a founder
- How they scaled the app to 20k users with a team of 2 people (1 engineer) by using the KISS principle
- How distribution is the most important thing for a micro-SaaS and why they decided to target the Shopify marketplace
- How they prioritize features and make their customers happy while having a very lean team
- How to acquire customers every day for the next year
- Why you should build a business that allows you to have freedom and live a good life
 - We also asked them if they ever received an offer to be acquired or to get VC funding

metadata.title: Micro-SaaS Sprint for Nomads: Build Low-Maintenance Recurring Revenue
metadata.author: Nomad Life Success
metadata.shortDescription: Tired of feast-or-famine freelance cycles and endless client firefights? In this episode Aria Reyes walks you through a realistic micro-SaaS sprint designed for American digital nomads who want reliable, low-touch recurring revenue without quitting client work or burning out. You’ll get a clear definition of what a viable micro-SaaS looks like for service-first nomads, a 3-step, AI-friendly launch blueprint you can execute alongside client projects, and a real-world nomad case study that shows how small subscription products stabilized income and reduced weekly client hours. The episode also covers how to scale the product with contractors and automation while protecting energy and travel flexibility. Finish with an immediate 48-hour validation task that proves demand before you invest time. Practical, conservatively paced, and focused on longevity—this is micro-product building with nomad life in mind.

segments.text: Let me tell you about three products that have almost nothing in common, except they
each crossed a million dollars in revenue with a team you could fit in a single elevator.
Nomad List. A spreadsheet about cities. Today it generates $5.3 million a year,
built and run almost entirely by one person. Carrd. A simple website builder, intentionally
stripped of features. It crossed $1.5 million in ARR and powered over 3 million websites.
TweetHunter. A tool that helped people grow on Twitter. Over $1 million ARR, two founders,
zero venture capital. No board meetings. No
fundraising rounds. No armies of engineers. Just one focused product, solving one specific
problem, for a very specific type of person. That is what Micro SaaS is all about…
And in 2026, it is one of the most accessible wealth-building models in the software industry.
In this video, we’ll talk about how you can build and launch your own micro saas product in 2026….
To begin with - What Is Micro SaaS and Why 2026 Is the Year to Build?
The global SaaS market is sitting at somewhere between $376 billion and $465 billion in 2026
depending on which research firm you ask. That number gets thrown around a lot. Here
is the one that actually matters for you: The Micro SaaS segment alone is growing
at 30% annually and is projected to reach $59.6 billion by 2030.
Micro SaaS is not a startup. It is not a platform. It is a focused, profitable software tool built
for a very specific audience — typically run by one to five people, typically generating between
$5,000 and $250,000 in monthly recurring revenue. The profit margins are the part that gets
founders. Traditional software businesses operate around 15 to 30 percent net margins.
Whereas In 2026, the average profit margin for a micro-SaaS business has risen to 45%,
while bootstrapped, single-founder products frequently operate at net margins between 70%
and 90% due to hyper-lean infrastructure. No office. No bloated headcount.
No enterprise sales cycles. And the build time has collapsed.
In 2026, the standard expectation for getting a product to initial launch is 8 to 12 weeks.
Two years ago, that same launch would have taken 6 to 24 months.
AI-assisted development, component libraries, and cloud infrastructure have changed math entirely.
So — one focused problem, a small paying audience,
recurring revenue, high margins, fast to ship. That is the complete game.
Now, the most challenging part is Finding Your Micro SaaS Idea the Right Way…
Here is the mistake almost every first-time founder makes: they sit down and try to
brainstorm a SaaS idea. Do not do that.
Good Micro SaaS ideas are not invented. They are found — in complaints, in workarounds,
in the stuff people are already cobbling together with spreadsheets and duct tape.
Where to hunt: Go to Reddit. Find the subreddits where
your target audience lives —Freelancers, Shopify sellers, agency owners, HR managers, whatever.
Try searching for words like "frustrated", "annoying", "why doesn't anyone make",
"I wish there was a tool for that." Read App Store reviews on tools in the
space you're considering. The one-star and two-star reviews are a goldmine.
People tell you exactly what is missing. Join relevant Slack communities and Discord
groups. Ask questions. Listen more than you talk. Once you find a recurring complaint,
apply this filter: "Would I pay $29 a month for a tool that fixed this?"
If the honest answer is yes — and more importantly, if the people in those communities
say yes — you have something worth investigating. Now The red flags to avoid are:
Ideas that are Too broad. "Project management for everyone" is a category, not a product.
Ideas that are Too niche. Twelve potential customers is a hobby, not a business.
Ideas that are Already dominated. If Notion, Monday.com, or any well-funded
giant has already solved this exact problem with a free tier, move on.
The sweet spot is a problem that is real, recurring, and underserved. A tool that a
specific type of business absolutely needs but that no major player has bothered to build well.
Now, the Next Challenge is Building It Without Building the Wrong Thing
A 2025 analysis of solo-founded Micro SaaS businesses found something uncomfortable:
30% never reach $1,000 in MRR and abandon the project entirely.
The most common reason is not bad code but building features no one asked for.
So before you write a single line of code —Validate.
The fastest validation method in 2026: Describe the product in a landing page.
Set up a waitlist. Share it in the communities where you found the problem.
If you cannot get 20 people to sign up in two weeks,
the idea needs to change — not the marketing copy.
Gil Hildebrand, the founder of Subscribr, pre-sold 50 lifetime deals and generated
$20,000 before writing any code. That is validation before investment.
Once you have a signal, build the smallest version of the product that delivers the core outcome.
One problem. One workflow. One result. Cut everything else.
We definitely need mention of vibe coding and AI-generated apps…
AI coding tools have made it faster than ever to get something running. That is real.
But there is a difference between a prototype and a production-ready product.
Buggy onboarding, insecure authentication, and poor database design will destroy
your retention before you ever get to grow. At iTechnoLabs, we have seen founders come to us
after launching an AI-generated MVP that worked in demos but fell apart under real user load.
Getting the engineering foundation right from the beginning is not optional,
but it is what separates products that grow from products that die after launch.
Key build decisions at the MVP stage include: One core use case only. Resist every temptation
to add "just one more feature." Charge from day one. Free plans
kill your ability to learn whether people actually value what you built.
Ship to 10 to 20 real users before any public launch. Their
feedback will reshape the product completely. How to Launch Your Micro SaaS Idea in the Market?
Firstly, You do not need 10,000 followers to launch a Micro SaaS product. You need the right
10 people to find you first. Here is the cold launch
playbook that actually works in 2026: Product Hunt. Still relevant, especially for
developer and productivity tools. A solid launch can drive 500 to 2,000 signups in a single day.
The preparation matters more than the launch day itself — line up your upvoters in advance.
Niche communities. Go back to the Reddit threads and Slack groups where you found
the problem. Share what you built. Be transparent about where it is in its development. Founders in
these communities respond to authenticity far better than polished marketing.
Founder Twitter and LinkedIn. Build in public. Share the journey — the metrics, the setbacks,
the wins. Searches for "micro SaaS examples" on Google are up 320% since 2022. People are
actively looking for this kind of content. Pricing — start higher than you think.
Most first-time founders underprice by a significant margin. The psychology behind
Micro SaaS pricing is this: if your tool saves someone two hours a week,
it is worth far more than $9 a month to them. Start at $29 to $49 a month. You can
always run a discount. You cannot easily raise prices once you've anchored expectations low.
One benchmark worth knowing: SaaS companies under $1 million in ARR posted a median growth
rate of 50% in 2024. The early stage moves fast when distribution is right.
Your first 10 customers matter more than your first 1,000 followers.
Talk to them. Get them on calls. Understand exactly how they use the product, what they skip,
and what they would pay more for. That information is worth more than any marketing campaign.
After Launch, How to Grow Your Micro SaaS Product to $5K MRR and Stay There?
See, Getting to your first $1,000 MRR is about finding the right people.
Getting to $5,000 MRR is about keeping them. Here is a number that most founders ignore
until it is too late: SMB SaaS products average 3 to 5% monthly churn. At 5% monthly churn,
your average customer is gone in 20 months. At 2%, that same customer stays for over four years.
The math compounds in both directions. A 2026 retention benchmark study found that
the median annual B2B SaaS retention sits around 88 to 90% for well-run products. Top performers
push Net Revenue Retention above 110% — meaning they are making more money from existing customers
every month even without adding new ones. Getting there requires three things:
Onboarding that delivers value fast. Research from 2026 shows that reducing time-to-first-value
to under 7 days is one of the highest-leverage retention investments you can make. If a user
does not experience the core outcome within their first week, the probability of them
cancelling spikes dramatically. One distribution channel, done
obsessively. The founders who grow fastest in Micro SaaS are rarely doing everything.
They are doing one channel — SEO, cold email, Product Hunt, community — and going deeper into
it every week. Spreading thin kills momentum. When to add features versus when to add
customers. The answer is almost always: add customers first. Features built for paying
users who are actively asking for them survive. Features built on founder intuition rarely do.
And here is the milestone framework worth tracking:
$1K MRR: product-market signal. You have something.
$3K to $5K MRR: proof of repeatable acquisition. $10K MRR: the point where most solo
founders consider going full-time. 95% of Micro SaaS businesses that reach
any revenue reach profitability within their first year. That is not startup mythology. That is the
structural advantage of a model built around low overhead, recurring revenue, and focused scope.
To summarize the five steps: Find the problem in the communities
where your audience lives. Validate before you build.
Ship the smallest version that delivers real value.

videos.full_text: Let me tell you about three products that have almost nothing in common, except they each crossed a million dollars in revenue with a team you could fit in a single elevator. Nomad List. A spreadsheet about cities. Today it generates $5.3 million a year, built and run almost entirely by one person. Carrd. A simple website builder, intentionally stripped of features. It crossed $1.5 million in ARR and powered over 3 million websites. TweetHunter. A tool that helped people grow on Twitter. Over $1 million ARR, two founders, zero venture capital. No board meetings. No fundraising rounds. No armies of engineers. Just one focused product, solving one specific problem, for a very specific type of person. That is what Micro SaaS is all about… And in 2026, it is one of the most accessible wealth-building models in the software industry. In this video, we’ll talk about how you can build and launch your own micro saas product in 2026…. To begin with - What Is Micro SaaS and Why 2026 Is the Year to Build? The global SaaS market is sitting at somewhere between $376 billion and $465 billion in 2026 depending on which research firm you ask. That number gets thrown around a lot. Here is the one that actually matters for you: The Micro SaaS segment alone is growing at 30% annually and is projected to reach $59.6 billion by 2030. Micro SaaS is not a startup. It is not a platform. It is a focused, profitable software tool built for a very specific audience — typically run by one to five people, typically generating between $5,000 and $250,000 in monthly recurring revenue. The profit margins are the part that gets founders. Traditional software businesses operate around 15 to 30 percent net margins. Whereas In 2026, the average profit margin for a micro-SaaS business has risen to 45%, while bootstrapped, single-founder products frequently operate at net margins between 70% and 90% due to hyper-lean infrastructure. No office. No bloated headcount. No enterprise sales cycles. And the build time has collapsed. In 2026, the standard expectation for getting a product to initial launch is 8 to 12 weeks. Two years ago, that same launch would have taken 6 to 24 months. AI-assisted development, component libraries, and cloud infrastructure have changed math entirely. So — one focused problem, a small paying audience, recurring revenue, high margins, fast to ship. That is the complete game. Now, the most challenging part is Finding Your Micro SaaS Idea the Right Way… Here is the mistake almost every first-time founder makes: they sit down and try to brainstorm a SaaS idea. Do not do that. Good Micro SaaS ideas are not invented. They are found — in complaints, in workarounds, in the stuff people are already cobbling together with spreadsheets and duct tape. Where to hunt: Go to Reddit. Find the subreddits where your target audience lives —Freelancers, Shopify sellers, agency owners, HR managers, whatever. Try searching for words like "frustrated", "annoying", "why doesn't anyone make", "I wish there was a tool for that." Read App Store reviews on tools in the space you're considering. The one-star and two-star reviews are a goldmine. People tell you exactly what is missing. Join relevant Slack communities and Discord groups. Ask questions. Listen more than you talk. Once you find a recurring complaint, apply this filter: "Would I pay $29 a month for a tool that fixed this?" If the honest answer is yes — and more importantly, if the people in those communities say yes — you have something worth investigating. Now The red flags to avoid are: Ideas that are Too broad. "Project management for everyone" is a category, not a product. Ideas that are Too niche. Twelve potential customers is a hobby, not a business. Ideas that are Already dominated. If Notion, Monday.com, or any well-funded giant has already solved this exact problem with a free tier, move on. The sweet spot is a problem that is real, recurring, and underserved. A tool that a specific type of business absolutely needs but that no major player has bothered to build well. Now, the Next Challenge is Building It Without Building the Wrong Thing A 2025 analysis of solo-founded Micro SaaS businesses found something uncomfortable: 30% never reach $1,000 in MRR and abandon the project entirely. The most common reason is not bad code but building features no one asked for. So before you write a single line of code —Validate. The fastest validation method in 2026: Describe the product in a landing page. Set up a waitlist. Share it in the communities where you found the problem. If you cannot get 20 people to sign up in two weeks, the idea needs to change — not the marketing copy. Gil Hildebrand, the founder of Subscribr, pre-sold 50 lifetime deals and generated $20,000 before writing any code. That is validation before investment. Once you have a signal, build the smallest version of the product that delivers the core outcome. One problem. One workflow. One result. Cut everything else. We definitely need mention of vibe coding and AI-generated apps… AI coding tools have made it faster than ever to get something running. That is real. But there is a difference between a prototype and a production-ready product. Buggy onboarding, insecure authentication, and poor database design will destroy your retention before you ever get to grow. At iTechnoLabs, we have seen founders come to us after launching an AI-generated MVP that worked in demos but fell apart under real user load. Getting the engineering foundation right from the beginning is not optional, but it is what separates products that grow from products that die after launch. Key build decisions at the MVP stage include: One core use case only. Resist every temptation to add "just one more feature." Charge from day one. Free plans kill your ability to learn whether people actually value what you built. Ship to 10 to 20 real users before any public launch. Their feedback will reshape the product completely. How to Launch Your Micro SaaS Idea in the Market? Firstly, You do not need 10,000 followers to launch a Micro SaaS product. You need the right 10 people to find you first. Here is the cold launch playbook that actually works in 2026: Product Hunt. Still relevant, especially for developer and productivity tools. A solid launch can drive 500 to 2,000 signups in a single day. The preparation matters more than the launch day itself — line up your upvoters in advance. Niche communities. Go back to the Reddit threads and Slack groups where you found the problem. Share what you built. Be transparent about where it is in its development. Founders in these communities respond to authenticity far better than polished marketing. Founder Twitter and LinkedIn. Build in public. Share the journey — the metrics, the setbacks, the wins. Searches for "micro SaaS examples" on Google are up 320% since 2022. People are actively looking for this kind of content. Pricing — start higher than you think. Most first-time founders underprice by a significant margin. The psychology behind Micro SaaS pricing is this: if your tool saves someone two hours a week, it is worth far more than $9 a month to them. Start at $29 to $49 a month. You can always run a discount. You cannot easily raise prices once you've anchored expectations low. One benchmark worth knowing: SaaS companies under $1 million in ARR posted a median growth rate of 50% in 2024. The early stage moves fast when distribution is right. Your first 10 customers matter more than your first 1,000 followers. Talk to them. Get them on calls. Understand exactly how they use the product, what they skip, and what they would pay more for. That information is worth more than any marketing campaign. After Launch, How to Grow Your Micro SaaS Product to $5K MRR and Stay There? See, Getting to your first $1,000 MRR is about finding the right people. Getting to $5,000 MRR is about keeping them. Here is a number that most founders ignore until it is too late: SMB SaaS products average 3 to 5% monthly churn. At 5% monthly churn, your average customer is gone in 20 months. At 2%, that same customer stays for over four years. The math compounds in both directions. A 2026 retention benchmark study found that the median annual B2B SaaS retention sits around 88 to 90% for well-run products. Top performers push Net Revenue Retention above 110% — meaning they are making more money from existing customers every month even without adding new ones. Getting there requires three things: Onboarding that delivers value fast. Research from 2026 shows that reducing time-to-first-value to under 7 days is one of the highest-leverage retention investments you can make. If a user does not experience the core outcome within their first week, the probability of them cancelling spikes dramatically. One distribution channel, done obsessively. The founders who grow fastest in Micro SaaS are rarely doing everything. They are doing one channel — SEO, cold email, Product Hunt, community — and going deeper into it every week. Spreading thin kills momentum. When to add features versus when to add customers. The answer is almost always: add customers first. Features built for paying users who are actively asking for them survive. Features built on founder intuition rarely do. And here is the milestone framework worth tracking: $1K MRR: product-market signal. You have something. $3K to $5K MRR: proof of repeatable acquisition. $10K MRR: the point where most solo founders consider going full-time. 95% of Micro SaaS businesses that reach any revenue reach profitability within their first year. That is not startup mythology. That is the structural advantage of a model built around low overhead, recurring revenue, and focused scope. To summarize the five steps: Find the problem in the communities where your audience lives. Validate before you build. Ship the smallest version that delivers real value. Launch to the right 10 people before you go wide. And Retain obsessively — because retention is what converts a product into a business. metadata.title: How to Win on Product Hunt in 2026 (from 6 Founders Who Did)
metadata.author: Unabyss
metadata.shortDescription:
How to Win on Product Hunt (from 6 Founders Who Did)

Launching on Product Hunt is seen as a huge opportunity to boost your startup. And almost nobody tells you what actually moves the needle - or whether it's even worth the effort.

So we gathered the people who've done it and asked them to share their experience.

6 founders whose products won on Product Hunt each share 1-2 tactics that actually helped them win, and what the win got them afterward. No theory, no recycled launch checklists - just what worked.

We also brought in two people who see this from the other side:
→ Rohan - Product Hunt's #1 hunter
→ Gabe - Head of Product Curation at Product Hunt

By the end, you'll know how to prep a launch that can win, and whether a PH launch is worth it for your product in the first place.

Building a SaaS to $5 million ARR usually requires a massive marketing budget and a bloated team. Marie and her partner did it with a team of two, zero paid ads, and a "build in public" mindset.
